docs.title: CI/CD Workflows Reference
docs.text: GitHub Actions workflow architecture, mechanics, and customization.

docs.title: Workflow Architecture
docs.text:
Orchestrator: - ci-cd.yml - Main workflow coordinating all jobs based on trigger event

Reusable Workflows: - config-summary.yml - Configuration and production mode detection - metadata-extract.yml - Build metadata extraction - docker-build.yml - Docker image build and push - pull-and-promote.yml - Image promotion between registries (production mode) - resolve-image-digest.yml - Digest lookup by tag (production mode) - smoke.yml - Post-deploy smoke tests against the live deployed revision - judge-eval.yml - LLM-as-judge behavioral gate, run in-process against the checked-out agent - require-stage-success.yml - Tag-time gate requiring the tagged SHA's stage run to have passed before prod promotion (production mode) - terraform-plan-apply.yml - Terraform deployment

Standalone CI Workflow: - ci.yml - Code quality (ruff, mypy, pytest with coverage), Postgres integration lane, and deterministic agent eval gate

Standalone Release Workflow: - release.yml - release-please: keeps the release pull request open and tags vX.Y.Z with a GitHub Release when it merges

Key principle: Infrastructure as code + GitOps = reproducible deployments.

docs.title: GitHub Variables (Auto-Created by Bootstrap)
docs.text:
Dev-only mode: - Variables scoped to the dev environment

Production mode: - Variables scoped to each environment (dev, stage, prod, prod-apply)

Jobs read these variables, and authenticate to GCP, only when they declare the matching environment:.

Variable Name Description GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT GCP project ID REGION GCP Compute region GOOGLE_CLOUD_LOCATION Vertex AI model endpoint routing IMAGE_NAME Docker image name (also agent_name) WORKLOAD_IDENTITY_PROVIDER WIF provider resource name ARTIFACT_REGISTRY_URI Registry URI ARTIFACT_REGISTRY_LOCATION Registry location TERRAFORM_STATE_BUCKET GCS bucket for main module state WORKLOAD_IDENTITY_POOL_PRINCIPAL_IDENTIFIER WIF principal identifier for main module IAM bindings OTEL_INSTRUMENTATION_GENAI_CAPTURE_MESSAGE_CONTENT GenAI message content capture mode

Note: These are Variables (not Secrets) because they're resource identifiers, not credentials. Security comes from WIF IAM policies.

docs.title: ci-cd.yml (Orchestrator)
docs.text:
Triggers: - Pull request to main (docs and local development changes excluded) - Push to main (docs and local development changes excluded) - Tag push matching prod-v* (a promotion tag on the commit a vX.Y.Z release tag marks; a v* tag alone starts no run). Release steps: Release a Version: Promote to Production

Key jobs: - changes - dorny/paths-filter resolving the deploy and eval filters that gate build and judge-eval (branch events only) - meta - Extract metadata (tags, SHA, context) - config - Determine production mode - build - Build Docker image (branch events only, not tags; gated on changes.outputs.deploy == 'true') - resolve-digest - Look up image in stage by tag (tag events in production mode) - dev-plan / dev-apply - Dev environment (branch events) - dev-smoke - Post-deploy smoke against the live dev revision (after dev-apply) - judge-eval - LLM-judge behavioral gate on merge (blocking in production mode, signal only in dev-only mode; gated on changes.outputs.eval == 'true') - stage-promote / stage-plan / stage-apply - Stage environment (merge in production mode) - stage-smoke - Post-deploy smoke against the live stage revision (after stage-apply, production mode only) - require-stage-success - Tag-time gate: requires the tagged SHA's merge run to have passed Apply Stage, Smoke Stage, and Judge Eval before promotion (production mode, upstream of prod-promote) - prod-promote / prod-plan / prod-apply - Prod environment (tags in production mode) - prod-smoke - Post-deploy smoke against the live prod revision (after prod-apply, production mode only)

Concurrency: - PR builds: Cancel in-progress on new push (cancel-in-progress: true) - Main builds: Run sequentially (no cancellation, cancel-in-progress: false) - Terraform applies queue per environment and plans never queue; the Terraform state lock serializes their state access (see terraform-plan-apply.yml)

Path filtering: the trigger paths-ignore exclusions prevent the workflow from running on docs or local development changes; the changes job selects which jobs run when the change set passes the trigger exclusions.

The trigger is a denylist, because the only thing it needs to answer is "could this possibly affect a deployment or a gate?" GitHub does not allow paths and paths-ignore on the same event, and a denylist is the correct polarity here: the list is short, provably non-deployable, and its failure direction is harmless. A path missing from it starts a run whose jobs all skip, costing seconds of runner time.

paths-ignore:
  - '*.md'
  - 'docs/**'
  - 'init_template.py'
  - 'mkdocs.yml'
  - 'LICENSE'
  - 'notebooks/**'
  - '.claude/**'
  - '.env.example'
  - '.pre-commit-config.yaml'

The Markdown pattern is shallow '*.md' and not recursive '**.md' to cover only the root files (README.md, AGENTS.md, CHANGELOG.md) and nothing else, while docs/** and .claude/** cover the Markdown that lives in those trees. A recursive '**.md' would also swallow Markdown a fork adds inside the package, like a prompt fragment or a skill definition under src/, and that file would silently stop triggering runs. Keeping the pattern shallow makes the safe behavior structural instead of something a fork has to remember.

The rest of the list is local-developer and template scaffolding with no CI or image role: init_template.py is the one-time bootstrap script, .pre-commit-config.yaml drives local hooks that no workflow invokes, and .env.example is a template for local .env. The Dockerfile copies only pyproject.toml, uv.lock, and src, so none of them can reach an image.

The changes job is the allowlist, and the only place that enumerates paths that do something. Allowlist is the correct polarity here for the opposite reason: a forgotten path means "no build", which is visible and safe, where a denylist controlling a deploy decision would fail open and roll out unchanged source. The action parses its filters input as YAML itself, so a YAML anchor removes the duplication that the workflow-level parser cannot (GitHub Actions rejects anchors in workflow syntax).

filters: |
  deploy: &deploy
    - 'src/**'
    # ...everything that lands in an image or the infrastructure running it
  eval:
    - *deploy
    - 'tests/eval/**'
    - '.github/workflows/judge-eval.yml'

build gates on deploy, judge-eval gates on eval. deploy lists every reusable workflow ci-cd.yml calls, tag-only ones included, so the rule stays uniform and a workflow-only edit lands on a commit that built an image and can be tagged. eval is a superset: a source or dependency change alters agent behavior, so the judge should score it too. tests/eval/** sits only in eval, which makes an eval-data merge score the change that altered what the gate asserts while building nothing. judge-eval scores the checked-out source in-process, so it depends on no image and no deploy job.

One condition on build is enough to skip the whole deploy chain: every deploy job reaches build through needs, and a skipped dependency skips its dependents.

The invariant between the layers: every paths-ignore entry must be absent from both filters. A path in both can never reach the allowlist, because the run never starts, and the allowlist entry is silently dead.

Tag pushes always run: GitHub does not evaluate path filters for them. The changes job is branch-only for the same reason, plus a tag push has no base to diff against.

docs.title: Workflow Flows
docs.text: Job-level dependency graphs showing how GitHub Actions jobs chain together. For the higher-level deployment strategy view, see Deployment Modes: Deployment Flow.

docs.title: PR Flow
docs.text:
Trigger: Push to feature branch with open PR

What happens (both modes): 

config (parallel root: selects mode, gates via if-conditions)
changes, metadata-extract ─→ docker-build → dev-plan

Result: Plan preview in PR comment, no actual deployment. A PR touching only tests/eval/** runs changes, meta, and config and skips the rest: there is no image to build and no plan to preview, and the judge gate is a merge-time job. The deterministic eval gate in ci.yml covers that PR.

docs.title: Merge Flow
docs.text:
Dev-only mode: 

changes, config ─→ judge-eval
changes, metadata-extract ─→ docker-build → dev-plan → dev-apply → dev-smoke

Production mode: 

changes, config ─→ judge-eval
changes, metadata-extract ─→ docker-build ┬─→ dev-plan → dev-apply → dev-smoke
                                          │
config ───────────────────────────────────┴─→ stage-promote → stage-plan → stage-apply → stage-smoke

Result: Dev deployed and smoked (always), stage deployed and smoked (production mode only), and the judge eval scored on every merge that touches the agent or its eval data. judge-eval runs from source rather than against a revision, so it starts as soon as changes and config resolve and never waits on a deploy. It blocks the merge run in production mode and is signal only in dev-only mode. The smoke lane detail lives in Smoke Tests; the eval lane's in Agent Evals.

Eval-data-only merge (both modes): 

changes, config ─→ judge-eval
changes ─→ (docker-build and every deploy job skipped)

eval matches and deploy does not, so the judge gate scores the change that altered what it asserts and nothing is rebuilt or redeployed. In production mode this merge run has no Apply Stage or Smoke Stage conclusion, so promoting that commit fails require-stage-success closed. That is correct, not a defect; see Require Stage Success.

docs.title: Tag Flow
docs.text:
Dev-only mode: 

config, metadata-extract → (no deploy)
Tags deploy nothing in dev-only mode: a v* release tag starts no run, and a prod-v* promotion tag runs only meta and config (build skips and dev-plan/dev-apply are branch-only). meta still validates the promotion tag, so a malformed one or one without its release tag on the same commit turns that run red. Dev-only mode deploys on merge to main, not on tags.

Production mode: 

metadata-extract ─┐
                  ├─→ resolve-digest ──────┐
config ──┬────────┘                        │
         │                                 │
         └─→ require-stage-success ────────┤
                                           ↓
                                 prod-promote → prod-plan → prod-apply → prod-smoke

require-stage-success gates the prod pipeline tag run. No eval runs at tag time; the gate reads the merge run's Judge Eval conclusion. See Require Stage Success for details.

Result: Version-tagged deployment, gated on stage success plus the behavioral judge gate, and smoked after apply. Prod requires an approval in the prod-apply environment from the reviewers bootstrap configures.

docs.title: Image Tagging Strategy
docs.text: Tags name images for people and for the tag-time digest lookup. Every deploy consumes an immutable digest, never a tag.

docs.title: Tags by Event
docs.text:
metadata-extract.yml derives the tag list. {sha} is the full 40-character commit SHA, so no two commits share it, and it always comes first, because resolve-image-digest.yml and the promotion digest check read the first tag. {sha7} in the PR tag is the first 7 characters of the PR head commit, for readability; nothing promotes PR images.

Event Registry Tags Written by Pull request dev pr-{number}-{sha7} (PR head commit, not the merge commit) build Merge to main dev {sha}, latest build Merge to main (production mode) stage {sha}, latest (same digest, copied) stage-promote Promotion tag (production mode) prod {sha}, latest, {version} (the release tag the promotion tag names, like v1.0.0 for prod-v1.0.0) prod-promote Every build dev buildcache (BuildKit layer cache, never deployed) build

latest is a convenience pointer that moves on every merge (and on every release in prod). No workflow reads it. buildcache is overwritten on every build; Image Digest Resolution describes the artifact.

docs.title: Build Once, Promote by Digest
docs.text:
1. Build (merge): build builds the image once, in dev, and pushes it with its tags. {sha} is applied at push time, before any smoke test has run against that digest.
  2. Promote to stage (merge, production mode): stage-promote copies the dev digest into the stage registry under the same tags with crane cp, then fails unless the target digest equals the source digest.
  3. Deploy: Terraform receives a digest URI (registry/image@sha256:...), so every Cloud Run revision pins a digest and every new digest creates a new revision. The deployed digest is the OCI index; revisions record the platform image digest inside it (Image Digest Resolution).
  4. Release (promotion tag, production mode): nothing rebuilds. resolve-digest reads the digest behind stage {sha}, require-stage-success confirms the tagged commit's merge run passed Apply Stage, Smoke Stage, and Judge Eval, and prod-promote copies that digest into prod with the {version} tag added. Prod then deploys the digest after the prod-apply approval.

Prod therefore runs a digest that stage deployed and smoked: the tag run promotes only what stage {sha} resolves to, require-stage-success ties that digest to a green stage smoke (Require Stage Success), and the copy and deploy steps preserve it byte for byte.

docs.title: Registry Tags Stay Mutable
docs.text:
The Artifact Registry repositories do not enable immutable tags. Deployment already consumes only immutable digests, {sha} is unique per commit, and require-stage-success proves the promoted digest is the one stage smoked, so registry-level immutability would guarantee nothing the pipeline does not already guarantee.

The setting is repository-wide, so enabling it would also reject the re-push of latest and buildcache on every build. Keeping it off preserves the registry build cache and the latest pointer at no correctness cost. The remaining way to repoint {sha} is a manual push to the registry, which Artifact Registry IAM governs.

docs.title: Re-running a Merge Run
docs.text:
require-stage-success reads the conclusions of the merge run's latest attempt, and stage {sha} is written only by that commit's own merge-run attempts. Any re-run is therefore safe for prod: a re-run that leaves stage on an unsmoked digest also leaves Smoke Stage not green, and the tag fails closed.

  • To re-validate the same image: use "Re-run failed jobs" on the merge run. Jobs that succeeded keep their results, and the re-run jobs work on the digest already built.
  • To rebuild: "Re-run all jobs" rebuilds from the same commit. With a warm buildcache every layer is cached and the digest is byte-identical; a cache miss produces a new digest, which moves {sha} in dev and stage, and that attempt's own stage smoke must pass before the commit can be released.
  • To ship a different image: land a new commit. A new image belongs to a new {sha}; never retag a digest by hand.

Promote a release only from a commit whose merge run's latest attempt is green.

docs.title: Registry Cleanup
docs.text:
The cleanup policies in terraform/bootstrap/module/gcp/main.tf decide how long a tagged image stays available. Retention values are set per environment in each bootstrap root's terraform.tfvars.

  • Untagged images are deleted. A digest that loses its last tag, like the previous image when a rebuild moves {sha}, is removed.
  • Tagged images age out too. The general retention policy deletes images older than registry_cleanup_general_retention_days, tagged or not, unless a KEEP policy (registry_cleanup_keep_count, or the buildcache keep) protects them. Artifact Registry applies a KEEP policy over a DELETE policy when both match (cleanup policies).
  • PR images expire separately when registry_cleanup_pr_retention_days is set (dev only).

Two consequences follow. Stage {sha} must still exist when you promote, or resolve-digest fails and the release stops before promotion; a release tag can sit unpromoted only as long as stage retention keeps its image. And re-deploying an older prod digest from the registry works only while that digest is retained, so size prod retention to your rollback window.

docs.title: Reusable Workflows
docs.text:
Caller constraints: a job that calls a reusable workflow may not set continue-on-error, env, steps, or timeout-minutes. Non-blocking behavior therefore has to be an input the called workflow honors by exiting 0 itself; judge-eval.yml's gating input is the instance.

Optional overrides: a workflow that takes an optional override resolves inputs.X || vars.X once in the job-level env: block and references ${{ env.X }} in its steps, like IMAGE_NAME: ${{ inputs.image_name || vars.IMAGE_NAME }} in docker-build.yml. The fallback is stated once and the steps never repeat it.

docs.title: config-summary.yml
docs.text:
Purpose: Determine deployment mode and create configuration summary.

Inputs: - production_mode (boolean) - Enable multi-environment deployment

Outputs: - production_mode - Pass-through for downstream jobs - Job summary with deployment mode explanation

When it runs: First job in every ci-cd.yml run

docs.title: metadata-extract.yml
docs.text:
Purpose: Extract build metadata (tags, SHA, context).

Outputs: - Image tags (PR, SHA, latest, version) - Build context (pull_request, push, tag) - Metadata summary

When it runs: After config job in ci-cd.yml

docs.title: docker-build.yml
docs.text:
Purpose: Build and push Docker images.

Inputs: - Image tags from metadata-extract.yml - Registry URI and location - Environment (dev/stage/prod)

Optional overrides (for subproject builds): - image_name - override vars.IMAGE_NAME - context - Docker build context path (defaults to .)

Features: - Builds for linux/amd64 (Cloud Run target platform) - Registry cache with protected buildcache tag - Build provenance and SBOM generation

Outputs: - Image digest (immutable identifier) - Digest URI (registry/image@sha256:...)

When it runs: After metadata extraction (branch events only, not tags)

docs.title: pull-and-promote.yml
docs.text:
Purpose: Promote images between registries (production mode only).

Inputs: - Source environment (dev or stage) - Target environment (stage or prod) - Source digest - Target tags

Optional overrides (for subproject promotion): - image_name - override vars.IMAGE_NAME for both source and target (image name is intended to remain static across environments)

How it works: 1. Authenticate to source and target registries via WIF 2. Pull image from source registry by digest 3. Re-tag image with all target tags 4. Push to target registry

Outputs: - Image digest (same as source) - Digest URI in target registry

When it runs: Production mode deployments (dev → stage, stage → prod)

docs.title: resolve-image-digest.yml
docs.text:
Purpose: Resolve image digest from tag (production mode only).

Inputs: - Environment (stage) - Tags to resolve

Optional overrides (for subproject digest lookup): - image_name - override vars.IMAGE_NAME for the resolved environment

How it works: 1. Authenticate to registry via WIF 2. Query Artifact Registry for image by tag 3. Extract digest (sha256:...)

Outputs: - Image digest - All tags associated with the image

When it runs: Production mode tag deployments (lookup stage image for prod)

docs.title: terraform-plan-apply.yml
docs.text:
Purpose: Plan and apply Terraform changes.

Inputs: - Environment (dev/stage/prod) - Action (plan/apply) - Docker image digest - WIF and state bucket details - save_plan (boolean) - Save plan artifact - use_saved_plan (boolean) - Use saved plan artifact

Features: - Plan artifacts saved between jobs (ensures plan matches apply) - PR comment with plan output (plan-only runs) - Job summary with deployment details - Terraform init, validate, plan, apply steps (formatting is checked by the pre-commit suite in ci.yml)

When it runs: After build (or promote) for each environment

Key behavior: - plan job on PR: Comment plan, don't save artifact - plan job on merge: Save plan artifact (no comment) - apply job: Use saved plan artifact

Concurrency and state locking: the terraform job sets its own concurrency group. An apply joins terraform-apply-<environment> with cancel-in-progress: false, so applies to one environment run one at a time and a running apply is never cancelled. Each plan gets a group unique to its run, so plans never queue behind each other or behind an apply.

GitHub keeps one running and one pending job per concurrency group, and a newly queued job cancels the pending one. A shared group for plans would let three PRs pushing together (a Dependabot batch, for example) cancel the middle plan, and would let a PR plan displace a merge's pending apply.

The GCS backend's state lock serializes the state access instead. Plan and apply both pass -lock-timeout=30m, so a run that finds the lock held waits for it rather than failing. Thirty minutes covers a plan waiting behind a full apply, including a first apply that creates the Cloud SQL instance, one of the slowest resources the main module creates. An apply waiting behind a few PR plans needs far less. A wait that runs past it fails with the lock holder's details in the log, which points at a stuck lock rather than ordinary contention. The job's 60-minute timeout-minutes sits above that worst case: the full lock wait followed by a first apply. An apply queued in its concurrency group has not started, so queue time does not count toward it. Keep the limit generous: a timeout that stops an apply partway can leave the state lock held and the apply half-done.

docs.title: smoke.yml
docs.text:
Purpose: Run the post-deploy smoke lane against the live deployed Cloud Run revision.

Inputs: - environment (dev/stage/prod) - selects the GitHub Environment vars and secrets - service_url - deployed Cloud Run URL, from the apply job's smoke_target_url output - invoker_service_account - invoker SA email to impersonate, from the apply job's smoke_invoker_service_account_email output

How it works: 1. Authenticate to GCP via WIF 2. Run uv run pytest tests/smoke with SMOKE_BASE_URL and SMOKE_INVOKER_SA set from the inputs, surfacing pass/fail in the job summary

The service deploys --no-allow-unauthenticated, so requests need a Cloud Run ID token. The lane mints one in-process by impersonating a dedicated invoker SA (the runner's WIF principal holds serviceAccountOpenIdTokenCreator on it), so no token crosses the environment. The service URL and SA email come from terraform-plan-apply.yml outputs. See Security Posture for the identity model. The lane layering and assertions live in Smoke Tests.

When it runs: Called by ci-cd.yml after each environment apply — dev-smoke after dev-apply on merge, and in production mode stage-smoke after stage-apply on merge and prod-smoke after prod-apply on tag. Not part of the PR gate.

docs.title: judge-eval.yml
docs.text:
Purpose: Run the LLM-as-judge behavioral gate (the judge marker in tests/eval) against the checked-out agent.

Inputs: - environment (dev/stage/prod) - selects the GitHub Environment vars and secrets, which supply the WIF principal and the Vertex AI project - gating (optional, default true) - whether a sub-threshold score fails the job

What gets scored is not an input. The eval set, the judge criteria, and the per-gate run counts are constants in tests/eval/test_agent_eval.py, so CI and a local run score the same thing and changing either is a reviewable code diff.

How it works: 1. Authenticate to GCP via WIF 2. Probe model liveness (-m "judge and liveness") under the default shell, so a dead endpoint fails the job in either mode 3. Run the scored eval (-m "judge and not liveness"), surfacing pass/fail in the job summary alongside the environment and whether the run was blocking

The eval runs in-process and App-aware, so it scores the same agent the built image carries without a deployed revision, a service URL, or invoker auth. ci-cd.yml passes environment: dev in both deployment modes: the job needs Vertex AI credentials rather than a deployed target, and dev keeps it clear of stage's deployment protection rules. The judge gate scores JUDGE_NUM_RUNS passes per case, set to 5 in the eval module because judge metrics return a binary verdict per run and 2 would quantize the average to 0, 0.5, or 1 — see Agent Evals. ADK runs those passes serially (num_runs is a for loop in AgentEvaluator; its parallelism semaphore fans out across eval cases, not runs), so wall clock scales linearly with the run count and sublinearly with case count.

gating exists because a job that calls a reusable workflow may not use continue-on-error. With gating: false the workflow reports the regression in the summary, emits a warning annotation, and exits 0, so the job conclusion stays success — which is what the dev-only mode wants, since nothing reads that conclusion there.

gating absorbs a sub-threshold score and nothing else. The preflight is a separate step, and the eval test leaves through EVAL_ERROR_EXIT_CODE (70, os.EX_SOFTWARE, "an internal software error was detected") when the eval could not run or any run went unscored, so the scored step's exit 1 can only be a sub-threshold verdict over fully scored runs. Every other non-zero exit (pytest's own 2 to 6, or 70 for an eval error or unscored run) fails the job in both modes, and the summary names the code. Malformed eval config or data fails at collection, inside the preflight step. Both steps pass -s, so the job log streams ADK's output as each run happens. Without that split, a dead judge endpoint would abort the lane with the same exit 1 as a regression and report green forever in dev-only mode, which is the vacuous pass the preflight was added to prevent.

When it runs: Called by ci-cd.yml as judge-eval on merge to main, blocking in production mode and signal only in dev-only mode. Not on PRs (the deterministic gate in ci.yml covers those) and not on tags.

Swapping the eval body: A consumer changes what is scored by editing tests/eval/data/ (the eval set and full_eval_config.json) and, for the file paths or run counts, the constants in tests/eval/test_agent_eval.py. The workflow takes no eval inputs, so there is nothing to override from the caller. Replacing the eval framework entirely (deepeval, ragas, or other) means pointing the judge-eval job at a different reusable workflow; the gate interface is just the job's name and conclusion, so require-stage-success needs no change as long as the job is still named Judge Eval.

docs.title: require-stage-success.yml
docs.text:
Purpose: Tag-time gate that requires the tagged SHA's stage release candidate to have passed before prod promotion.

Inputs: - head_sha - the tagged commit whose stage run is required to have passed (github.sha on the tag event) - stage_run_workflow (optional, default ci-cd.yml) - the workflow whose merge-to-main run deployed stage

How it works: 1. Find the merge run for head_sha on the default branch (the tag run is excluded because its head branch is the tag ref) 2. Require that run's Apply Stage, Smoke Stage, and Judge Eval jobs all concluded success (matching the reusable-workflow X / <inner> job-naming; anything but success, including skipped, fails closed)

Judge Eval covers the behavioral dimension: it scores the same commit's agent code in-process, so requiring its conclusion gates the behavior the promoted digest carries without depending on the stage rollout. A behavioral regression reds the merge run after stage has already deployed, which blocks the prod tag rather than reverting stage.

Stage success is the whole prod gate for image fidelity. The promotion workflow copies the image digest-for-digest and prod deploys by digest, so prod runs exactly the digest resolve-digest reads from stage {sha} — the fidelity guarantee lives there, not in this gate. So the gate only has to confirm that digest was validated, and a green Smoke Stage does: stage {sha} is written only by that commit's own merge-run attempts, the tag run never rebuilds (it only re-reads {sha} and promotes it), and the jobs API reports the latest attempt, so a green smoke means {sha} resolves to the digest that was smoked. No separate digest comparison is needed (and conclusions, not outputs, are what the REST API exposes after a run). The only way to break that equivalence is an out-of-band registry repoint of {sha}, governed by Artifact Registry IAM. Because prod-promote declares needs: require-stage-success, a failure halts the tag run upstream of the prod-apply approval.

Tagging a commit that built no image. Not every merge produces an image. A merge touching only tests/eval/** runs the judge gate and skips build, so Apply Stage and Smoke Stage are skipped in that run and this gate fails closed on them. It's intentional behavior: no image exists for that commit, so stage {sha} resolves to nothing and prod's deploy-by-digest has nothing to promote. Relaxing the gate to accept a skipped stage job would trade a clear failure for an unsound pass.

Practically, a release belongs on a commit whose merge deployed and smoked stage. If the last merge before a release changed only eval data, tag the commit before it, or land a deployable change first.

Permissions: actions: read (read the merge run's job conclusions), contents: read. No GCP credentials.

When it runs: Called by ci-cd.yml on tag events in production mode, before prod-promote. Generic and agent-agnostic, so every fork inherits it.

docs.title: ci.yml
docs.text:
Purpose: Run the pre-commit hook suite and pytest with coverage, the Postgres integration lane, and the deterministic agent eval gate.

Pipeline (five jobs): 1. changes - dorny/paths-filter detects whether relevant files changed 2. code-quality - runs every pre-commit hook on all files (uv run pre-commit run --all-files --show-diff-on-failure: ruff, mypy, actionlint, terraform fmt, config-file checks), then pytest with coverage even when a hook fails. Installs Terraform from .terraform-version for the fmt hook and caches hook environments. Restores .mypy_cache on every run so mypy re-checks only what changed, and saves it only on pushes to main: pull requests read main's cache without adding entries to the repository's Actions cache quota. Runs on every push and pull request, since the hooks cover every file type. Checks out with persist-credentials: false, since the hooks run third-party code. 3. integration - runs pytest tests/integration, which starts a throwaway postgres:18 via testcontainers on the runner's Docker daemon (no coverage gate; the 100% gate is unit-lane-only). The postgres:18 image matches the deployed Cloud SQL POSTGRES_18 major. Gated on changes.outputs.code == 'true'. 4. agent-eval - runs the deterministic agent eval (uv run pytest tests/eval -m "deterministic") against Vertex AI, authenticating with the dev environment's WIF principal (no coverage gate). Gated on changes.outputs.code == 'true'. 5. status - always-runs sentinel that aggregates results for branch protection

Timeout: 10 minutes each for the code-quality, integration, and agent-eval jobs (typical: 2-3 minutes)

When it runs: Every push to main and every pull request. code-quality always runs; integration and agent-eval are skipped when no code paths changed; the status sentinel always reports.

Branch protection: Require CI / status (the status job). The sentinel requires code-quality to pass, and integration and agent-eval to pass or be skipped because no code paths changed.

docs.title: release.yml
docs.text:
Purpose: Run release-please, which keeps one release pull request open with the next version and changelog, and tags vX.Y.Z and publishes a GitHub Release when that pull request merges.

Pipeline (one job): mint a token from the release GitHub App (RELEASE_APP_CLIENT_ID variable, RELEASE_APP_PRIVATE_KEY secret), then run googleapis/release-please-action with it. The App token makes the release pull request start ci.yml, so its required checks report; pull requests opened with GITHUB_TOKEN start no workflows. The workflow token itself has no permissions.

When it runs: Every push to main. The job is skipped when RELEASE_APP_CLIENT_ID is unset, so a fork without the App gets no failed runs. ci-cd.yml ignores the v* tag it creates; the release commit deploys through the normal merge run, and promotion uses prod-vX.Y.Z.

Setup, release steps and the changelog mapping: Release a Version.

docs.title: Workflow Behavior
docs.text:
Build cache: - Registry cache with protected buildcache tag - Significant speedup on cache hits - Never expires (protected by cleanup policy in bootstrap)

Timeouts: see each workflow's timeout-minutes; a job without one gets GitHub's 360-minute default. The Terraform job's limit is sized against the state-lock wait (see Concurrency and state locking above).

docs.title: Job Summaries
docs.text:
Workflows generate formatted summaries in GitHub Actions UI:

Config summary: - Deployment mode (dev-only vs production) - Environment deployment plan - Mode switching instructions

Metadata extraction: - Build context (PR, main, tag, manual) - Branch/tag name and commit SHA - All image tags (bulleted list)

Terraform deployment: - Environment and action (plan/apply) - Docker image being deployed - Step outcomes (init, validate, plan, apply) - Deployed resources (Cloud Run URL, Cloud SQL, Agent Engine, GCS bucket, bastion instance/zone) - Collapsible plan output

Job summaries provide quick insight without log analysis.

Writing a summary step: stream command output to the log and capture it in one pass with FILE=$(mktemp), cmd | tee "$FILE", and ${PIPESTATUS[0]} for the command's own exit code (tee's would always be 0). Export GitHub context to shell variables first, capture each value once, and check for empty outputs before rendering. smoke.yml and judge-eval.yml follow this pattern.

docs.title: PR Comments
docs.text:
Terraform plan workflow posts formatted comments on PRs:

Comment includes: - Plan summary (resources to add/change/destroy) - Collapsible sections for detailed output - Init and validation results - Full plan output

Permissions: Requires pull-requests: write in ci-cd.yml (configured).

docs.title: Authentication
docs.text:
Workload Identity Federation (WIF): - Keyless authentication (no service account keys) - GitHub Actions requests OIDC token - GCP validates against WIF provider - Grants temporary credentials only to jobs from this repository that run under the environment's GitHub Environments

IAM roles: See terraform/bootstrap/module/gcp/main.tf for complete role list.

Security: - Attribute condition on repository ID and GitHub Environment, so a job needs a matching environment: to authenticate (Security Posture Identity Layer) - Minimal permissions (only required roles) - Environment isolation (production mode, separate projects) - Cross-project IAM is registry-scoped (not project-level)

docs.title: Action and Hook Pinning
docs.text:
Every external action in .github/workflows/ is pinned to a full 40-character commit SHA, with the release it resolves to in a trailing comment:

- uses: actions/checkout@<40-char-sha>  # vX.Y.Z

Remote pre-commit hooks follow the same rule. Each rev in .pre-commit-config.yaml is a commit SHA with a # frozen: comment, the format pre-commit autoupdate --freeze writes, and CI runs these hooks too:

- repo: https://github.com/<owner>/<repo>
  rev: <40-char-sha>  # frozen: vX.Y.Z

Why pin by SHA: a tag like @v6 is mutable. Its owner, or anyone who compromises the owner's account, can repoint it, and these workflows hold id-token: write and federate to GCP, so an action running in them can mint cloud credentials. A SHA pin also stops a new release from changing what CI runs with no diff in this repository. GitHub's security hardening guide recommends SHA pinning for this reason.

Scope: every action from another repository, actions/* and google-github-actions/* included. Local reusable-workflow calls (uses: ./.github/workflows/*.yml) stay unpinned because they resolve to the caller's own commit.

Updates: Dependabot (.github/dependabot.yml) opens PRs on each entry's schedule, one grouped PR per entry unless noted, through four ecosystems: github-actions bumps each action SHA and its version comment together, and pre-commit reads each hook's # frozen: comment to pick the next release tag, then rewrites the SHA and the comment. uv bumps Python packages in uv.lock (minor and patch updates in one grouped PR, each major in its own, widening the upper bound in pyproject.toml, and open security fixes in one PR outside the schedule, with google-adk excluded from both groups so each ADK bump gets its own PR), and terraform bumps provider versions in terraform/main and, through a separate entry, the bootstrap roots (Infrastructure: Upgrading Provider Lockfiles). All four use the same cooldown, the exclude-newer window in pyproject.toml plus one day, so actions, hooks and Python packages wait out the same release age before adoption (Dependabot counts whole days, so the same number could admit a release up to a day younger). Dependabot does not touch a with: input, so a setup-uv step's version: input stays put, held to [tool.uv] required-version.

Adding an action or hook: resolve the release tag to its commit and pin that, never a branch or a floating major tag. For a hook, uv run pre-commit autoupdate --freeze --repo <url> resolves and writes both. For an action, or to check a hook by hand, dereference an annotated tag object to its commit:

gh api repos/<owner>/<repo>/git/ref/tags/<tag> --jq '.object.type + " " + .object.sha'
# If the type is "tag", resolve the tag object to its commit
gh api repos/<owner>/<repo>/git/tags/<sha> --jq '.object.sha'

docs.title: Change Deployment Mode
docs.text:
Edit production_mode in .github/workflows/ci-cd.yml:

jobs:
  config:
    uses: ./.github/workflows/config-summary.yml
    with:
      production_mode: true  # or false for dev-only

See Deployment Modes for complete instructions.

docs.title: Add Environment Variables
docs.text:
Runtime config (LOG_LEVEL, SERVE_WEB_INTERFACE, etc.): 1. Settings → Environments → {environment} → Environment variables 2. Add or edit variable 3. Re-run deployment or push new commit

Infrastructure config (CORS origins, etc.): 1. Edit terraform/main/main.tf 2. Create PR 3. Merge PR → deploys via CI/CD

See Deployment Modes for runtime vs infrastructure distinction.

docs.title: Add Build Steps
docs.text: Edit .github/workflows/ci-cd.yml or reusable workflows: - Code quality checks → Edit ci.yml - Integration tests → Add job after docker-build in ci-cd.yml - Custom notifications → Add to orchestrator

docs.title: Subproject Builds
docs.text:
The reusable workflows (docker-build.yml, pull-and-promote.yml, resolve-image-digest.yml) accept optional image_name and (for docker-build.yml) context overrides. This lets a single ci-cd.yml orchestrate multiple images, like a primary app plus a sidecar/relay subproject under relay/.

Pattern: add a parallel build-<name> job per subproject in ci-cd.yml, calling docker-build.yml with the subproject's image_name and context. Mirror with parallel promote/resolve jobs (same image_name override) and pass each resulting digest_uri through to terraform-plan-apply.yml as a new TF_VAR_* input.

Path filters: add the subproject's context path to the changes job's deploy filter and gate the new job on needs.changes.outputs.deploy == 'true' like build, or give the subproject its own filter output if it should build independently of the main app. Nothing to add at the trigger, which ignores documentation rather than allowlisting code, but confirm the new path is not swallowed by an existing paths-ignore entry.

Sub-context .dockerignore gotcha: Docker reads .dockerignore from the context root, not the repo root. When context: relay, the build sees relay/.dockerignore (if it exists) and ignores the project-root .dockerignore. Add a <context>/.dockerignore per subproject if you need exclusions.

CI lane per subproject: for code-quality coverage of a subproject, copy ci.yml to ci-<name>.yml, scope its paths-filter and step working-directory to the subdir, give the workflow a unique name: so its status check is uniquely addressable, and add the new <Name> / status to branch protection (bootstrap path: Protection Strategies Prerequisites).

No registry override: the parameterization deliberately stops at image_name (and context for builds). vars.ARTIFACT_REGISTRY_URI embeds the per-env GCP project, and GitHub Environment vars resolve in the callee's env context (not the caller's), so a static input override would defeat per-env isolation and break cross-project promotion. Subprojects therefore land in the same per-env Artifact Registry as the main app, distinguished only by image_name. If a subproject genuinely needs a different per-env registry, define a new env-scoped GitHub var in bootstrap and consume it directly in a per-subproject reusable workflow rather than threading it through the existing inputs.

docs.title: Modify Triggers
docs.text:
Edit .github/workflows/ci-cd.yml triggers:

on:
  pull_request:
    branches: [main]
    paths-ignore:
      - '*.md'
      # Add more non-deployable paths (keep both lists identical)
  push:
    branches:
      - main
      # Add more branches
    paths-ignore:
      - '*.md'
    tags:
      - 'prod-v*'
      # Add more tag patterns

Adding a path here only stops runs from starting. To change what a run does, edit the changes job's deploy or eval filter; see Path filtering. Never put a path in both, or the allowlist entry becomes unreachable.
