docs.title: Code Quality
docs.text: Detailed code quality tools, enforcement strategies, and exclusion guidelines.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Tools to enforce code quality: 1. Ruff - Fast linting and formatting (replaces flake8, isort, black) 2. Mypy - Static type checking 3. Pytest - Testing with coverage

All configured in pyproject.toml.

Note

THIS GUIDE IS A TEMPLATE Replace {your_agent} found throughout the guide with your package name (e.g., my_custom_agent)

docs.title: Running Quality Checks
docs.text:
Each tool, in suite order: 

# Lint with ruff auto-fix first (security, bugs, style violations)
uv run ruff check --fix

# Then format, so the formatter sees the auto-fixed code
uv run ruff format

# Type check
uv run mypy

# Tests with coverage
uv run pytest --cov

On every commit: once installed (uv run pre-commit install), the hooks in .pre-commit-config.yaml run the lint, format, and type-check tools above in this order on the staged files, plus any other checks the config defines. CI runs the same hooks over the whole tree, which you can reproduce on demand: 

uv run pre-commit run --all-files

Before pushing: run the tests, which the hooks do not: 

uv run pytest --cov
Plus any other test lanes the project defines, like integration tests.

Order matters: everything that rewrites files finishes before anything that only reads them. ruff check --fix can change layout the formatter must then normalize, and mypy should check the final source. pyproject.toml does not set ruff's fix = true, so a bare ruff check (no --fix) only reports.

docs.title: What We Enforce
docs.text:
From pyproject.toml: 

[tool.ruff.lint]
select = [
    "E",   # pycodestyle errors (PEP 8 violations)
    "W",   # pycodestyle warnings
    "F",   # pyflakes (unused imports, undefined names)
    "I",   # isort (import sorting)
    "B",   # flake8-bugbear (common bugs and design problems)
    "C4",  # flake8-comprehensions (better list/dict comprehensions)
    "UP",  # pyupgrade (modern Python syntax)
    "N",   # pep8-naming (naming conventions)
    "S",   # flake8-bandit (security issues)
    "SIM", # flake8-simplify (code simplification)
    "PTH", # flake8-use-pathlib (use Path instead of os.path)
]

Key enforcements: - E501: Line too long (88 characters) - PTH (pathlib rules): Use pathlib.Path instead of os.path - PTH123: Use Path.open() instead of open() - PTH118: Use Path.joinpath() instead of os.path.join() - Why: Modern API, cross-platform, chainable (path / "subdir"), type-safe - Ruff auto-fixes many os.path calls to Path - S (security rules): Catch common security issues - S101: Use of assert (banned in production, allowed in tests via per-file ignore) - S104: Binding to 0.0.0.0 (flagged for security, intentional in containers) - S105: Possible hardcoded password (detects patterns like "password = 'secret'")

docs.title: Per-file Exclusions
docs.text:
From pyproject.toml: 

[tool.ruff.lint.per-file-ignores]
"tests/**/*.py" = ["S101"]  # Allow assert statements in tests

Why: Tests use assert for validation. This is standard pytest practice and not a security concern.

docs.title: Inline Exclusions
docs.text:
Real example from our codebase: 

# tests/unit/conftest.py
mock_credentials.token = "test-mock-token-totally-not-real"  # noqa: S105

Rule: S105 (Possible hardcoded password) Why excluded: This is a test mock credential, not a real secret. The string content makes it obvious it's not production.

Real example from tests: 

# tests/unit/test_config.py
"HOST": "0.0.0.0",  # noqa: S104

Rule: S104 (Binding to all interfaces) Why excluded: Docker containers need to bind to 0.0.0.0 to accept connections from the host. This is intentional and documented.

When to use # noqa: - Security rules (S*) with false positives on test code - Line length (E501) for URLs or data that can't be split - Specific rule violation that's intentional and safe

Prefer specific rule codes: 

# Good - clear what's being suppressed
url = "https://example.com/very/long/api/path"  # noqa: E501

# Avoid - unclear what's being allowed
some_code()  # noqa

Use # noqa only when: - Rule violation is intentional and well-justified - Auto-fix would make code less readable - External constraint prevents compliance (e.g., third-party API format)

docs.title: Ruff Auto-fix
docs.text:
Ruff can automatically fix many issues:

# Auto-fix all fixable issues
uv run ruff check --fix

# Preview fixes without applying (safe mode)
uv run ruff check --diff

What gets auto-fixed: - Import sorting (rule I) - Unused imports (rule F401) - Whitespace and indentation (rules E, W) - Quote style normalization (rules Q) - Trailing commas (rules COM) - Simple code transformations (e.g., os.path.join() → Path.joinpath())

What requires manual fixing: - Complex logic issues - Security concerns (rule S) - Naming violations (rule N) - Code simplification requiring logic changes (rule SIM)

Best practice: 1. Run uv run ruff check --fix first (auto-fixes linting issues) 2. Run uv run ruff format second (formats the fixed code) 3. Review remaining issues and fix manually

docs.title: What We Enforce
docs.text:
From pyproject.toml: 

[tool.mypy]
plugins = ["pydantic.mypy"]
python_version = "X.Y"  # follows .python-version
# Tests are namespace packages (no __init__.py), so module names come from paths
explicit_package_bases = true
mypy_path = "src"
files = ["src", "tests"]
strict = true
warn_unused_configs = true
warn_unreachable = true

strict = true turns on mypy's maintained strict flag set, and picks up new checks as mypy adds them to it. See --strict for the current list. warn_unreachable sits outside that set, so it is enabled on its own. The pydantic plugin checks model construction, like ServerEnv(...), against the declared field types.

Key enforcements: - Every function needs complete annotations (args + return) - def foo(x: str = None) is an error (must use str | None) - Returning Any from a typed function is flagged (type safety leak) - if my_str == 5: is an error (comparing incompatible types) - Unused # type: ignore comments and redundant casts are errors - Names imported from a package that does not explicitly re-export them are errors (no_implicit_reexport). Import from the defining submodule instead, like google.adk.tools.function_tool rather than google.adk.tools - Dead code after returns/raises is flagged (warn_unreachable)

docs.title: Example Errors and Fixes
docs.text:
Error: missing return annotation (no-untyped-def) 

# mypy error: Function is missing a return type annotation
def process_data(items: list[str]):
    return len(items)


# Fixed
def process_data(items: list[str]) -> int:
    return len(items)

Error: partially annotated function (no-untyped-def) 

# mypy error: Function is missing a type annotation for one or more arguments
def fetch_user(id: int, cache):
    return cache.get(id)


# Fixed
def fetch_user(id: int, cache: dict[int, User]) -> User | None:
    return cache.get(id)

Error: implicit None default (assignment) 

# mypy error: Incompatible default for argument (expected str, got None)
def greet(name: str = None) -> str:
    return f"Hello, {name or 'stranger'}"


# Fixed - explicit None in union
def greet(name: str | None = None) -> str:
    return f"Hello, {name or 'stranger'}"

docs.title: Test Suite Typing Strategy
docs.text:
mypy checks tests/ alongside src/, with two overrides:

[[tool.mypy.overrides]]
# Test functions take fixtures by name without annotations
module = "tests.*"
disable_error_code = ["arg-type", "no-untyped-def", "no-untyped-call"]

[[tool.mypy.overrides]]
# Fixture definitions stay fully typed
module = "tests.*.conftest"
enable_error_code = ["no-untyped-def", "no-untyped-call"]
Disabled code Why no-untyped-def pytest injects fixture parameters by name, not by type. Annotating test function parameters adds ceremony without signal. no-untyped-call Follows from the above: calling an unannotated test helper from a typed function. arg-type Duck-typed mocks (like MockMemoryCallbackContext) intentionally stand in for real types in tests.

Every other strict check applies to tests. The second override re-enables the annotation checks for conftest.py files, so fixture definitions carry full annotations (MockerFixture in, MockType out) and an unannotated fixture fails mypy. It must use enable_error_code: a narrower section's disable_error_code does not undo codes a broader matching section disabled.

@pytest.fixture
def mock_state(mocker: MockerFixture) -> MockType:
    """Mock state with test data."""
    state: MockType = mocker.Mock(spec=State)
    return state

Patterns the strict checks shape in tests: - Annotate a mocker.Mock(...) result before returning it. mypy infers it as Any, so a direct return mocker.Mock(...) from a -> MockType fixture fails no-any-return. - Call a -> None function without capturing its result. result = callback(...); assert result is None fails func-returns-value, and mypy already proves the None return from the signature. - Patch a module attribute with mocker.patch.object(module, "name", ...), not module.name = value. Assignment to a name the module does not re-export fails attr-defined; the string form also restores the original on teardown. Session-scoped fixtures use pytest-mock's session_mocker. - Narrow parsed data with isinstance() before returning it as a concrete type. yaml.safe_load and json.loads return Any. - Third-party packages without type information get a narrow ignore_missing_imports override in pyproject.toml, with a comment naming why. Check first whether a newer release or a stub package (types-*) supplies types.

docs.title: Inline Exclusions
docs.text:
When you might need # type: ignore: 

# Third-party library without type stubs
import untyped_library  # type: ignore[import-untyped]

# Mypy bug or limitation (add TODO)
result = complex_function()  # type: ignore[return-value]  # TODO: Fix when mypy supports this pattern

Always prefer: 1. Fix the actual type issue (restructure code to make types clear) 2. Add type stubs for third-party libraries 3. Use type narrowing - validate types at runtime with isinstance() checks or type guards

Never use cast() - use type narrowing instead:

Why cast() is bad: - Bypasses type safety: Tells mypy to trust you without verification - Runtime risk: No runtime validation - type mismatch crashes at runtime - Dishonest about code behavior: Hides the actual types being used - Maintenance burden: Future changes break assumptions silently

Type narrowing is always better: 

# Bad - using cast() (DON'T DO THIS)
from typing import cast

result = some_function()
value = cast(str, result)  # Trust me, it's a string! (no runtime check)

# Good - type narrowing with isinstance()
result = some_function()
if not isinstance(result, str):
    raise TypeError(f"Expected str, got {type(result)}")
value = result  # mypy knows this is str now, AND we validated at runtime

Type narrowing keeps you honest about what the code actually does - it satisfies both mypy and provides runtime safety.

docs.title: Workflow Lint and Version Pins
docs.text:
actionlint runs only as a pre-commit hook, so its rev in .pre-commit-config.yaml is the single version pin and CI enforces it through the code-quality pre-commit step, with no separate job or Docker image. actionlint also runs shellcheck over inline run: blocks, but only when shellcheck is on PATH. The CI runner always has it, so CI's result is deterministic; a machine without it skips the pass, and its findings surface only in CI. Quote expansions (SC2086) and group consecutive appends to one file into { ...; } >> "$FILE" (SC2129); where grouping would hurt readability, use a # shellcheck disable=SC2129 on that one command with the reason beside it, never a file-wide directive. zizmor (template injection, unpinned actions, excessive permissions) is a separate audit with its own findings and is not part of the actionlint hook.

Terraform is pinned once, in .terraform-version (exact X.Y.Z). tenv reads it locally. hashicorp/setup-terraform has no version-file input, so each workflow step that installs Terraform is preceded by a step that reads the file into an output. TestTerraformVersionPin in tests/unit/test_pinned_versions.py fails if a workflow hard-codes terraform_version. Each root's required_version stays a range.

docs.title: What We Enforce
docs.text:
From pyproject.toml: 

[tool.coverage.run]
source = ["src"]
branch = true  # Check both line and branch coverage

[tool.coverage.report]
fail_under = 100  # Require 100% coverage

100% coverage is non-negotiable for production code.

docs.title: File-level Exclusions
docs.text:
From pyproject.toml: 

[tool.coverage.run]
omit = [
    # server.py: wiring run at import (settings, telemetry, ADK app); smoke lane
    "src/**/server.py",
    # agent.py: App and LlmAgent composition; eval lane
    "src/**/agent.py",
]

A file is omitted only when it is wiring with no logic of its own and another test lane runs it for real. Each comment names that lane: - server.py: builds the app at import, after settings and telemetry setup. The smoke lane exercises it on the deployed service; a unit test would only re-check the wiring with every dependency mocked. - agent.py: composes the App and LlmAgent. The eval lane runs it against a real model.

Everything else is measured, including __init__.py (its PEP 562 lazy loader is real branching logic) and prompt.py. Pattern: test every new file; omit one only when it meets the same bar, and name the lane in its comment.

docs.title: Line-pattern Exclusions
docs.text:
When a measured file gains lines that never run under test, exclude those lines by pattern instead of omitting the file. Add the pattern to [tool.coverage.report] exclude_also in pyproject.toml when the code first appears. Common patterns:

[tool.coverage.report]
exclude_also = [
    'if __name__ == "__main__":',  # script guard
    "if TYPE_CHECKING:",           # type-checker-only imports
    "@overload",                   # typing overload stubs
    "raise NotImplementedError",   # abstract method bodies
]

The template sets none today: no measured file contains these lines. See coverage.py: Excluding code.

docs.title: Inline Exclusions
docs.text:
Real example from our codebase: 

# src/{your_agent}/config.py (ServerEnv.allow_origins_list)
if not isinstance(result, list):  # pragma: no cover
    # Pydantic validation makes this unreachable
    msg = "Invalid allow_origins format"
    raise TypeError(msg)

Why: The @field_validator above this property ensures result is always a list. This defensive check exists for static type safety but is unreachable at runtime. Pydantic guarantees it.

When to use # pragma: no cover: - Defensive code (provably unreachable) needed to satisfy the static type-checker - Platform-specific branches not testable in CI (e.g., Windows-only code) - Error paths that require external system failures (rare)

When NOT to use it: - "This is hard to test" - write better tests or use better code patterns to facilitate testing - "Coverage is annoying" - coverage is finding gaps as intended - Normal error handling - always test error paths

docs.title: When to Run Checks
docs.text:
On every commit: the pre-commit hooks run lint, format, and type checks automatically.

Before pushing: uv run pytest --cov, plus any other test lanes the project defines.

During development: - Run ruff check --fix and ruff format frequently as you code - Run mypy after adding new functions or changing signatures - Run tests after behavior changes

IDE Integration: - Configure your editor to run ruff format on save - Enable mypy real-time checking for immediate feedback - Use pytest plugin for test execution and debugging

CI Enforcement: All checks run automatically in GitHub Actions on every PR: - Code quality workflow runs ruff, mypy, pytest - Blocks merge if any check fails - Ensures main branch always passes quality gates

docs.title: Why These Standards?
docs.text:
Strict typing (mypy): - Catch bugs before runtime - Enable powerful IDE features - Document code contracts - Facilitate safe refactoring

100% coverage: - Confidence in changes - Forces thinking about edge cases - Documents all code paths - Prevents untested code accumulation

Automated formatting (ruff): - Eliminates style debates - Consistent codebase - Fast code review - Auto-fix reduces friction

Security checks (bandit via ruff): - Catch common security mistakes - Enforce safe defaults - Educate developers on risks

docs.title: When to Add Exclusions
docs.text:
Never add exclusions: - To make broken code pass checks - Because it's "too much work" - For personal style preference - To ship faster without fixing issues

Acceptable exclusions: - Third-party library limitations (document why, add TODO if fixable) - Tool bugs (add TODO to fix when tool updates) - Provably unreachable defensive code (rare, requires strong justification) - Test-specific patterns (e.g., assert in tests, mock credentials)

Best practices: 1. Be specific: Use rule codes (# noqa: S105) not blanket suppression (# noqa) 2. Document why: Add comment explaining the exclusion 3. Add TODOs: If it's a workaround, plan to fix it later 4. Review regularly: Remove exclusions when underlying issue is fixed

Always prefer fixing the issue over adding exclusions.

← Back to References | Documentation

docs.title: Deployment Modes Reference
docs.text: Multi-environment deployment strategy, infrastructure parity, and image promotion.

docs.title: Dev-Only Mode (Default)
docs.text:
Infrastructure: - Single GCP project - Single Terraform deployment environment (dev) - One GitHub Environment variable scope - No tag protection

Workflow: - PR → dev plan (comment on PR) - Merge → dev deploy - Tags start no deployment

Use cases: - Experiments and prototypes - Internal tools with limited user base - Cost optimization (single project) - Rapid iteration without approval gates

Configuration: 

# .github/workflows/ci-cd.yml
jobs:
  config:
    uses: ./.github/workflows/config-summary.yml
    with:
      production_mode: false

docs.title: Production Mode (Opt-In)
docs.text:
Infrastructure: - Three GCP projects (dev/stage/prod) - Four GitHub Environments (dev/stage/prod/prod-apply) - Environment-scoped variables - Tag protection ruleset (admin-only prod-v* promotion tags)

Workflow: - PR → dev plan (comment on PR) - Merge → dev + stage deploy (parallel) - prod-vX.Y.Z promotion tag → prod deploy (manual approval required)

Use cases: - Customer-facing production services - Compliance requiring staged deployment - Infrastructure validation before production - Rollback capability critical

Configuration: 

# .github/workflows/ci-cd.yml
jobs:
  config:
    uses: ./.github/workflows/config-summary.yml
    with:
      production_mode: true

docs.title: Switching Modes
docs.text:
Requirements: 1. Bootstrap Github Environment(s) and Google Cloud project(s) for target mode 2. Configure protection rules (if switching to production mode) 3. Create PR with mode change in ci-cd.yml 4. Merge PR to apply new workflow behavior

Why config job parameter? GitHub Actions doesn't allow accessing workflow-level env variables (like env.PRODUCTION_MODE: {true/false})in jobs that call reusable workflows. The config job output pattern works around this limitation.

docs.title: Infrastructure Parity
docs.text:
All environments use identical infrastructure configuration. Stage validates the exact infrastructure that will deploy to prod.

Differences between environments: - Resource names (via environment variable: dev/stage/prod) - Runtime app config (GitHub Environment variables: LOG_LEVEL, etc.) - Cleanup policies (configured per environment in bootstrap)

Infrastructure config is hard-coded in Terraform and identical across environments. This ensures infrastructure changes (for example, the Cloud Run service minimum instance count) require explicit file edits and PR review, not hidden variable overrides.

docs.title: Deployment Flow
docs.text: For detailed job-level dependency graphs, see CI/CD Workflows: Workflow Flows.

docs.title: Dev-Only Mode
docs.text:
Pull Request: - Build Docker image → Plan infrastructure (no apply) - Comment plan on PR

Merge to main: - Build Docker image → Plan infrastructure → Apply to dev → Smoke test

Tag push: - No effect on deployment in dev-only mode

docs.title: Production Mode
docs.text:
Pull Request: - Build Docker image → Plan infrastructure (no apply) - Comment plan on PR

Merge to main: - Build Docker image, then in parallel: - Deploy to dev → Smoke - Deploy to stage → Smoke

Promotion tag push (prod-vX.Y.Z): - Verify staged image exists and stage run passed (parallel gates) → Deploy to prod (manual approval) → Smoke

Key principles: - Dev deployment never waits for stage or prod - Stage validates every merge (continuous feedback) - Prod deploys only on an explicit prod-vX.Y.Z promotion tag, pushed by a repository admin on the commit a vX.Y.Z release tag marks (release discipline). Commands: Release a Version: Promote to Production - Prod promotion is gated on the tagged commit's stage run passing (see CI/CD Workflows: Require Stage Success) - Uniform plan → apply pattern across all environments

docs.title: Image Promotion
docs.text: Production mode uses image promotion (pull from source, push to target) instead of rebuilding.

docs.title: Dev → Stage
docs.text:
Trigger: Merge to main

Process: 1. Build job pushes image to dev registry: us-central1-docker.pkg.dev/dev-project/agent-dev/image@sha256:abc123 2. stage-promote job: - Authenticates to dev and stage registries via WIF - Pulls image from dev registry by digest - Re-tags with all source tags - Pushes to stage registry: us-central1-docker.pkg.dev/stage-project/agent-stage/image@sha256:abc123

Cross-project IAM: - Stage WIF principal has roles/artifactregistry.reader on dev registry - Configured via promotion_source_* variables in stage bootstrap

docs.title: Stage → Prod
docs.text:
Trigger: Promotion tag push (like prod-v1.0.0) on the commit the v1.0.0 release tag marks

Process: 1. resolve-digest job: - Queries stage registry for the image by the commit's {sha} tag - Extracts digest: sha256:abc123 2. require-stage-success job (gates prod-promote): - Confirms the tagged commit's merge run had Apply Stage, Smoke Stage, and Judge Eval all succeed - Fails closed otherwise, halting the tag run before the prod-apply approval 3. prod-promote job: - Authenticates to stage and prod registries via WIF - Pulls image from stage registry by digest - Re-tags with all source tags - Pushes to prod registry: us-central1-docker.pkg.dev/prod-project/agent-prod/image@sha256:abc123

Cross-project IAM: - Prod WIF principal has roles/artifactregistry.reader on stage registry - Configured via promotion_source_* variables in prod bootstrap

docs.title: Why Promote Instead of Rebuild?
docs.text:
Guarantees: - Deploy the exact bytes that were tested in previous environment - No build-time differences (dependencies, base images, timestamps) - Immutable artifacts (can't accidentally rebuild with different code)

Performance: - Faster than rebuild (just pull/tag/push) - No dependency resolution, no layer builds

Consistency: - Same image digest across all environments - Easy to trace: "prod is running the same image validated in stage"

docs.title: Runtime vs Infrastructure Config
docs.text:
Runtime app config (configurable via GitHub Environment variables): - LOG_LEVEL - Logging verbosity - SERVE_WEB_INTERFACE - Enable web UI - OTEL_INSTRUMENTATION_GENAI_CAPTURE_MESSAGE_CONTENT - GenAI message content capture mode

GitHub Environment Variables pass overrides to Terraform as TF_VAR_* inputs. Default values managed in Terraform.

Terraform applies each override through coalesce(), so an empty or unset variable falls back to the default. docker_image is nullable: a run with no new image (an infrastructure-only apply) reuses the image from the previous deployment's state.

Infrastructure config (managed exclusively in Terraform files): - SESSION_SERVICE_URI - Session persistence URI (auto-created, postgresql+asyncpg:// protocol via Cloud SQL) - MEMORY_SERVICE_URI - Memory persistence URI (auto-created, agentengine:// protocol) - ARTIFACT_SERVICE_URI - GCS bucket URL (auto-created) - ALLOW_ORIGINS - CORS origins for Cloud Run - Terraform-managed values only (no variable overrides)

Why separate them: - Runtime config changes don't require Terraform rebuilds (fast iteration) - Infrastructure changes require explicit code review and PR (security) - CORS origins not overridable by GitHub variables (prevent bypass)

docs.title: Changing Runtime Config
docs.text:
Update GitHub Environment variables (no code changes):

  1. Settings → Environments → {environment} → Environment variables
  2. Edit or add unset variable (e.g., LOG_LEVEL=DEBUG or SERVE_WEB_INTERFACE=TRUE)
  3. Re-run latest workflow or push new commit

Changes apply on next deployment.

docs.title: Changing Infrastructure Config
docs.text:
Edit Terraform files and create PR:

git checkout -b fix/update-cors-origins
# Edit terraform/main/main.tf (e.g., update ALLOW_ORIGINS list)
git commit -m "fix: update CORS origins"
git push origin fix/update-cors-origins
gh pr create
# Review plan in PR comment
# Merge PR → deploys to dev (+ stage in production mode)

docs.title: Bootstrap Module
docs.text:
Purpose: One-time CI/CD infrastructure setup (per environment)

Location: terraform/bootstrap/{dev,stage,prod}/

Resources created: - Workload Identity Federation (keyless GitHub Actions auth) - Artifact Registry (Docker image storage with cleanup policies) - GitHub Environments (dev/stage/prod/prod-apply in production mode) - GitHub Environment Variables (auto-configured per environment) - Tag Protection (promotion tag ruleset, prod bootstrap only) - Cross-Project IAM (Artifact Registry reader for promotion, stage/prod)

State management: Remote state in GCS (per environment, bootstrap/ prefix). Pre-bootstrap (terraform/bootstrap/pre/, local state) creates the state buckets used by bootstrap and the main module.

Runs: Manually by infrastructure owners (one-time setup)

docs.title: Main Module
docs.text:
Purpose: Application deployment (runs in CI/CD)

Location: terraform/main/

Resources created: - VPC network + subnet + Private Services Access (Cloud SQL private IP) - Cloud NAT router (bastion outbound connectivity) - IAP firewall rules (SSH + SQL proxy port to bastion) - Bastion host (e2-micro, COS, Auth Proxy via cloud-init, dedicated SA with roles/iam.serviceAccountTokenCreator on app SA for impersonation). COS cloud-init opens port 5432 via iptables (default INPUT policy is DROP), configures --address=0.0.0.0 (accept IAP tunnel from non-loopback), and --impersonate-service-account=<app-sa-email> (IAM database auth as app SA). - Cloud Run Service (Auth Proxy sidecar + direct VPC egress) - Service Account (IAM identity for Cloud Run) - Cloud SQL instance (private IP only, session persistence via DatabaseSessionService) - Vertex AI Agent Engine (memory persistence) - GCS Bucket (artifact storage) - Cloud Monitoring alert policies (dry-run latency, traffic, errors, saturation and unhealthy instances, monitoring.tf)

State management: Remote state in GCS (bucket created by pre-bootstrap; bootstrap publishes its name as the TERRAFORM_STATE_BUCKET GitHub Variable)

Runs: Automatically in GitHub Actions on merge/tag

Inputs: All via TF_VAR_* environment variables from GitHub

Auth Proxy flags: local.cloud_sql_proxy_args holds the flags shared by the Cloud Run sidecar and the bastion. The bastion-only flags (--address=0.0.0.0, --impersonate-service-account) and the iptables rule live in templates/bastion-cloud-init.yaml.

IAM layering: each environment has its own GCP project. Project-level WIF roles are same-project only and live in terraform/bootstrap/module/gcp/. Cross-project Artifact Registry reader grants for promotion live in the stage and prod bootstrap roots. App service account roles live in terraform/main/main.tf, and consumer-added WIF roles in terraform/main/iam.tf.

Startup probes: the app container's startup probe polls /health for up to ~120s (24 failures x 5s) to cover credential initialization. The Auth Proxy sidecar has no startup probe; Cloud Run restarts it on crash, which is more reliable than probing it. When the app works locally but fails on Cloud Run, suspect credentials or VPC egress first.

docs.title: Resource Naming
docs.text:
All resources named: ${var.agent_name}-${var.environment}

Examples: - Cloud Run service: my-agent-dev, my-agent-stage, my-agent-prod - Artifact Registry: my-agent-dev, my-agent-stage, my-agent-prod - Service account: my-agent-dev@project.iam.gserviceaccount.com

Note: Service account IDs truncate agent_name to 30 chars (GCP limit).

docs.title: Docker Compose Workflow
docs.text: Running the local agent against deployed resources (Cloud SQL through the bastion, Agent Engine, GCS) with Docker Compose. For local sessions and artifacts with in-process memory, use uv run server (Development: Local Development).

docs.title: Start the Stack
docs.text:
Requires the deployed-resource values in .env and roles/iap.tunnelResourceAccessor (Development: Connect to Deployed Resources).

docker compose up --build --watch

Why both flags? - --build: Ensures you have the latest code and dependencies - --watch: Enables file sync with auto-restart for fast feedback

What happens: - Container starts with your latest code - Watch mode monitors your files for changes - Edits to src/ files are synced and the app restarts (no rebuild needed) - Changes to pyproject.toml or uv.lock trigger automatic rebuild

Leave it running while you work; changes apply automatically.

docs.title: Start with file sync and auto-restart (default workflow)
docs.text: docker compose up --build --watch

docs.title: Stop the service
docs.text:
# Press Ctrl+C to gracefully stop
# Or in another terminal:
docker compose down

docs.title: View logs
docs.text:
# If running in detached mode
docker compose logs -f

# View just the app logs
docker compose logs -f app

docs.title: Rebuild without starting
docs.text: docker compose build

docs.title: Run without watch mode
docs.text: docker compose up --build

docs.title: How Watch Mode Works
docs.text:
Watch mode uses the configuration in compose.yml:

develop:
  watch:
    # Sync + restart: copy changed files in, the image imports from /app/src
    - action: sync+restart
      path: ./src
      target: /app/src

    # Rebuild: Triggers full image rebuild
    - action: rebuild
      path: ./pyproject.toml

    - action: rebuild
      path: ./uv.lock

docs.title: Sync + Restart Action
docs.text:
• Triggers when: You edit files in src/
  • What happens: Files are synced into running container, then container restarts on the same image
  • Speed: About 3 seconds from save to a healthy app (2.6-3.3s over five edits on an arm64 laptop)
  • Use case: Code changes during development

docs.title: Rebuild Action
docs.text:
• Triggers when: You edit pyproject.toml or uv.lock
  • What happens: Image rebuilds from the dependency step on, container recreated on the new image
  • Speed: About 18 seconds from save to a healthy app (17.6s and 18.8s on an arm64 laptop with a warm uv cache)
  • Use case: Dependency changes

docs.title: IAP Tunnel to Bastion
docs.text:
Docker Compose uses an IAP tunnel container to reach the bastion host, which runs Cloud SQL Auth Proxy. This mirrors the production architecture where Cloud Run connects to Cloud SQL via private IP, but substitutes IAP tunneling for direct VPC egress.

Architecture: 

App container (localhost:5432) ──► IAP tunnel container ──► IAP ──► Bastion VM (Auth Proxy) ──► Cloud SQL private IP

The bastion Auth Proxy binds to 0.0.0.0 (not loopback) to accept IAP tunnel connections arriving from outside the loopback interface. It also uses --impersonate-service-account=<app-sa-email> to authenticate to Cloud SQL as the app SA, since the bastion runs under its own dedicated SA. These flags are bastion-specific — the Cloud Run sidecar uses the defaults (loopback binding, runs as app SA directly).

Restart policies differ by role: - App container (restart: no): Crash once, stay down. Keeps stack trace output clean for debugging — no restart noise to scroll past. - IAP tunnel (restart: unless-stopped): Auto-reconnect on network drops (laptop sleep, transient IAP failures). Infrastructure plumbing you don't want to babysit.

IAP tunnel container (gcr.io/google.com/cloudsdktool/google-cloud-cli:stable): - Uses network_mode: "service:app" to share the app container's network namespace — the tunnel binds to 0.0.0.0:5432 which appears as localhost:5432 from the app's perspective - Runs gcloud compute start-iap-tunnel targeting the bastion host on port 5432 - Requires BASTION_INSTANCE, BASTION_ZONE, and GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT in .env

Credentials: Mounts ~/.config/gcloud to /gcloud-config with CLOUDSDK_CONFIG=/gcloud-config (decouples from container home directory). IAP tunnel requires full gcloud CLI config, not just Application Default Credentials.

Developer IAM prerequisite: roles/iap.tunnelResourceAccessor on your Google account. Without this role, the IAP tunnel fails to connect.

Port: 5432 on the app container's localhost. The app connects to localhost:5432 identically to Cloud Run, where the Auth Proxy sidecar also listens on the same address.

Requires: BASTION_INSTANCE and BASTION_ZONE set in .env (get from deployment job summary or terraform output bastion_instance / terraform output bastion_zone).

docs.title: Connecting a local DB client
docs.text:
The app service publishes 127.0.0.1:5432:5432, so a database client on your host (psql, a GUI, migration tooling) can reach Cloud SQL through the same tunnel: the published port forwards into the app namespace where the IAP tunnel binds 0.0.0.0:5432, then on through the bastion Auth Proxy. Connect as the app SA: the bastion proxy impersonates it (--impersonate-service-account) and logs in with IAM database authentication (--auto-iam-authn), so no password is needed:

psql "host=127.0.0.1 port=5432 user=<app-sa-email-without-.gserviceaccount.com> dbname=agent_sessions sslmode=disable"

sslmode=disable is the setting the proxy expects (the bastion's own bootstrap connects the same way): the Auth Proxy encrypts the connection to Cloud SQL, and the laptop-to-bastion hop runs inside the IAP tunnel. The same roles/iap.tunnelResourceAccessor prerequisite applies.

Note

The compose services publish on their default host ports (8000 app, 5432 Postgres), all bound to 127.0.0.1. If one is already in use on your host (a local Postgres on 5432 is the common case), docker compose up fails to bind. Remap the host side of the affected ports: entry (like 127.0.0.1:5433:5432); the container-side port and the app's in-namespace localhost:5432 path are unaffected.

docs.title: Source Code
docs.text:
• Host: ./src/
  • Container: /app/src
  • Sync: Automatic via watch mode

docs.title: Credentials
docs.text:
• App container: ~/.config/gcloud/application_default_credentials.json mounted read-only at /gcloud/application_default_credentials.json — for Vertex AI and telemetry export via GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS
  • IAP tunnel container: Full ~/.config/gcloud/ directory mounted (writable) at /gcloud-config/ with CLOUDSDK_CONFIG=/gcloud-config — decouples from container home directory, writable because gcloud CLI writes token cache and logs at runtime, IAP tunnel requires full gcloud CLI config beyond ADC

docs.title: Environment Variables
docs.text:
Docker Compose loads .env automatically. See Environment Variables Guide for details on required and optional variables.

Note: The container uses HOST=0.0.0.0 to allow connections from the host machine.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: See Troubleshooting: Docker Compose for container restart issues, IAP tunnel failures, permission errors, port conflicts, and Windows path compatibility.

docs.title: Testing Registry Images
docs.text:
For rare cases when you need to test the exact image from CI/CD:

# Authenticate once
gcloud auth configure-docker us-central1-docker.pkg.dev

# Set your image
export REGISTRY_IMAGE="us-central1-docker.pkg.dev/project/repo/app:sha123"

# Pull and run it with your local settings and credentials
# (CI publishes linux/amd64 only; the flag lets Apple silicon pull it)
docker pull --platform linux/amd64 $REGISTRY_IMAGE
docker run --rm --platform linux/amd64 \
  --mount type=bind,source=$HOME/.config/gcloud/application_default_credentials.json,target=/gcloud/application_default_credentials.json,readonly \
  -e GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS=/gcloud/application_default_credentials.json \
  -p 127.0.0.1:8000:8000 \
  --env-file .env \
  $REGISTRY_IMAGE

docs.title: Direct Docker Commands (Without Compose)
docs.text:
If you need to build and run without Docker Compose:

docker build -t your-agent-name:latest .

# Startup needs Application Default Credentials (telemetry export uses them)
docker run --rm \
  --mount type=bind,source=$HOME/.config/gcloud/application_default_credentials.json,target=/gcloud/application_default_credentials.json,readonly \
  -e GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS=/gcloud/application_default_credentials.json \
  -p 127.0.0.1:8000:8000 \
  --env-file .env \
  your-agent-name:latest

Both docker run recipes on this page differ from Compose:

  • No IAP tunnel: a SESSION_SERVICE_URI pointing at localhost:5432 fails on the first session request. Unset it to store sessions inside the container (lost when the container is removed), or use Compose for Cloud SQL
  • --env-file keeps quotes: Docker passes KEY='value' with the quotes included, while Compose and python-dotenv strip them. Remove the quotes from values like ALLOW_ORIGINS or startup validation fails

They mount credentials with --mount rather than -v, so a missing credentials file fails the command instead of being created as an empty directory. Run gcloud auth application-default login first.

Note: Docker Compose is recommended - it handles volumes, environment, and networking automatically.

docs.title: Dockerfile Strategy Explained
docs.text: How and why to build a multi-stage uv Dockerfile.

docs.title: Table of Contents
docs.text:
• Overview
  • Dockerfile Breakdown
  • Why We COPY Instead of Using Bind Mounts
  • Rebuild and Push Cost
  • Summary
  • Local Development
  • References

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Our Dockerfile uses a multi-stage build with the following architecture:

  1. Builder Stage: python:X.Y-slim + uv binary (copied from Astral's distroless image)
  2. Runtime Stage: Clean python:X.Y-slim + the virtual environment and the source, as separate layers

X.Y is the Python version pinned in .python-version.

This approach gives us: - ✅ Official uv binary (pinned for reproducible builds) - ✅ No uv, uv cache or build metadata in the runtime image - ✅ Small pushes: a source edit changes only the source layer (kilobytes); the dependency layer stays cached - ✅ Runs as a non-root user

docs.title: Syntax Directive
docs.text:
# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1
What: Selects the Dockerfile frontend: the latest stable 1.x syntax Why: Builds get current Dockerfile features without upgrading Docker. BuildKit itself is already Docker's default builder, so docker build needs no flag or DOCKER_BUILDKIT=1 (Dockerfile reference)

docs.title: Builder Stage Base Image
docs.text:
FROM python:X.Y-slim AS builder
What: Start builder stage with official Python slim image (Debian-based), tagged with the version in .python-version Why: We need: - Python runtime for uv sync to work - Shell and basic utilities (cp, mkdir, etc.) for build commands

Why not ghcr.io/astral-sh/uv as base? - Astral's uv image is distroless: it contains only the uv and uvx binaries, so there is no shell to run RUN commands - It's designed to copy the binary FROM, not build FROM

docs.title: Copy UV Binary
docs.text:
COPY --from=ghcr.io/astral-sh/uv:X.Y.Z /uv /uvx /bin/
What: Extract just the uv and uvx binaries from Astral's image Why: - Pinned to an exact version for reproducible, deterministic builds (bump procedure: docs/development.md uv Version) - Copies two binaries, not a whole base image - Puts them in /bin/ so they're in PATH

docs.title: Working Directory
docs.text:
WORKDIR /app
What: Both stages work in /app. Each FROM starts a fresh filesystem, so the runtime stage sets it again.

docs.title: UV Environment Variables
docs.text:
ENV UV_LINK_MODE=copy \
    UV_COMPILE_BYTECODE=1 \
    UV_PYTHON_DOWNLOADS=never
What: Configure uv behavior Why:

Variable Value Reason UV_LINK_MODE=copy Copy files instead of hardlinking The cache mount and .venv are on separate filesystems, so uv can't hardlink and would warn UV_COMPILE_BYTECODE=1 Pre-compile .py → .pyc files Tends to improve startup time, at the cost of install time and image size (uv Docker guide) UV_PYTHON_DOWNLOADS=never Don't download Python Use system Python from base image

docs.title: Install Dependencies
docs.text:
COPY pyproject.toml uv.lock ./
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.cache/uv \
    uv sync --locked --no-install-project --no-dev
What: Install dependencies WITHOUT installing the project itself Why: This is the only install step. The project is never installed, so .venv holds dependencies only and changes only when pyproject.toml or uv.lock does.

Flag Meaning Benefit --mount=type=cache Persist /root/.cache/uv across builds Don't re-download packages already cached --locked Validate lockfile matches pyproject.toml Fails the build on a stale lockfile --no-install-project Skip installing the project package .venv stays independent of source edits --no-dev Skip dev dependencies Smaller image

Why --locked, not --frozen: a uv.lock that no longer matches pyproject.toml is a broken config. --locked fails the build loudly so it gets fixed; --frozen trusts the lockfile blindly, stale or not, so a mismatch ships undetected. The Dockerfile and every CI uv sync use --locked, as does uv's own GitHub Actions example.

# A dependency was added to pyproject.toml without re-running uv lock
$ docker build .
error: The lockfile at `uv.lock` needs to be updated, but `--locked` was provided.
$ uv lock && docker build .  # succeeds

What the cache mount buys: packages already downloaded are not fetched again. The gain is modest: most of a dependency install goes to unpacking and byte-compiling, not downloading. It also persists only on the same builder: cache-to exports layers, not cache mounts, so each CI run on a fresh runner starts with an empty uv cache (Docker GitHub Actions cache). Registry layer cache still skips the whole sync when pyproject.toml and uv.lock are unchanged.

docs.title: Runtime Stage Base
docs.text:
FROM python:X.Y-slim AS runtime
What: Start fresh with clean Python image for runtime Why: - uv, its cache and the dependency files stay in the builder stage - Runtime has only Python, .venv (from the builder) and src/ (from the build context)

docs.title: Non-Root User
docs.text:
RUN groupadd -g 10001 app && useradd -u 10001 -g app -M -s /usr/sbin/nologin app
What: Create a non-root user named app with a fixed UID and GID of 10001 Why: The server doesn't need root, so it doesn't run as root

Command breakdown: - groupadd -g 10001 app: Create the app group with GID 10001 - useradd -u 10001 -g app -M -s /usr/sbin/nologin app: Create the app user with UID 10001 in that group - -M: Create no home directory; the server writes nothing to ~/ - -s /usr/sbin/nologin: The account has no login shell, so su app or any login as app is refused. docker exec and the CMD start their own process and never read the account's shell, so the server and debugging sessions are unaffected

Why a fixed ID: volume mounts and file ownership on shared storage key on the numeric UID and GID, so a pinned value gives them a stable target that doesn't shift with the base image's user list. 10001 sits outside the range Linux hosts assign to people (the first user is usually 1000), so the container process never shares an ID with a host account. On native Linux Docker, a bind-mounted host file readable only by your host user (like a 0600 credentials file) may be unreadable to UID 10001.

docs.title: Copy Virtual Environment and Source
docs.text:
COPY --from=builder --chown=app:app /app/.venv ./.venv
COPY --chown=app:app src ./src
What: Copy the dependencies from the builder and the source straight from the build context, as two layers Why: - Each COPY produces one layer, and any change to its content invalidates the whole layer. The .venv layer is hundreds of MB; the src layer is tens of kB - A source edit rebuilds and re-pushes only the src layer; the .venv layer stays cached locally and in the registry. Copying /app in one layer would re-export and re-push the whole venv on every source edit - --chown=app:app: Make the app user own both - Only src/ comes from the build context: documentation, tests and config changes never invalidate a layer - uv, pyproject.toml and uv.lock are NOT copied (needed only to build)

Running from source: the package is imported from /app/src (see PYTHONPATH below), so code that locates files relative to __file__ sees the same src/<package>/ layout as a local checkout. Without a project install, the container venv has no [project.scripts] console scripts and no package metadata for the project (importlib.metadata cannot find it): start the app with python -m, and don't read the project's version from installed metadata at runtime.

docs.title: Runtime Environment
docs.text:
ENV VIRTUAL_ENV=/app/.venv \
    PATH="/app/.venv/bin:$PATH" \
    PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1 \
    PYTHONPATH=/app/src \
    HOST=0.0.0.0 \
    PORT=8000
What: Configure runtime environment Why:

Variable Purpose VIRTUAL_ENV=/app/.venv Tell Python which venv to use PATH="/app/.venv/bin:$PATH" Make venv binaries available (python, uvicorn) PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1 Don't buffer stdout/stderr (better logs in Docker) PYTHONPATH=/app/src Import the package from source, since the project is not installed HOST=0.0.0.0 Bind all interfaces so the server accepts connections from outside the container PORT=8000 Default port, matching EXPOSE

docs.title: Switch to Non-Root
docs.text:
USER app
What: All subsequent commands, and the container process at runtime, run as app

docs.title: Expose Port
docs.text:
EXPOSE 8000
What: Document the server's listening port (the PORT default above) Why: - Documentation only: it publishes nothing. Compose publishes through ports: in compose.yml, Cloud Run through the service's container port - docker run -P publishes exposed ports to random host ports

docs.title: Startup Command
docs.text:
CMD ["python", "-m", "<package>.server"]
What: Default command when container starts Why: - python -m runs the module directly, so no console script is needed (the project isn't installed) - Exec form (JSON array): Python runs as PID 1 and receives SIGTERM directly; the shell form would wrap it in /bin/sh -c, which does not pass signals (Dockerfile reference)

docs.title: Why We COPY Instead of Using Bind Mounts
docs.text:
uv's Docker guide also shows bind-mounting pyproject.toml and uv.lock into the sync step instead of copying them:

RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.cache/uv \
    --mount=type=bind,source=pyproject.toml,target=pyproject.toml \
    --mount=type=bind,source=uv.lock,target=uv.lock \
    uv sync --locked --no-install-project

Both invalidate the same way: BuildKit tracks bind-mounted files, so changing one re-runs the step. The only difference is that COPY leaves the two files (about 435 kB) in a builder layer. The builder stage never ships, so that costs nothing in the runtime image. We keep COPY because it is the plainer pattern.

docs.title: Rebuild and Push Cost
docs.text:
Once images build in CI and push to a registry, the cost of a change is the bytes it re-pushes, not local build time. Each change invalidates only its own layer and those after it:

Change Layers rebuilt and re-pushed Order of magnitude (compressed) Source edit in src/ src only kilobytes pyproject.toml or uv.lock dependency sync, .venv, src tens of MB Anything outside pyproject.toml, uv.lock and src/ none (never copied into the image) none

Compressed sizes are the size of each layer in the image's platform manifest in the registry; docker history shows uncompressed sizes. Layer sizes move with the dependency tree.

Alternatives considered:

Approach Why we don't use it Single stage Ships uv, its cache and build metadata in the runtime image One COPY /app . in the runtime stage A source edit re-pushes the whole venv layer Installing the project into .venv Writes source into .venv, so every source edit invalidates the venv layer Bind mounts for dependency files Same caching; saves only builder-stage bytes that never ship uv distroless image as base No shell for build commands

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Component Approach Why uv binary Copy from distroless (pinned) Reproducible builds, bump manually Base image python:X.Y-slim Need shell + Python for build, minimal for runtime Build pattern Multi-stage Discard uv, its cache and build metadata Dependency caching Cache mount Skip re-downloading cached packages Dependency files COPY both A change to either re-runs the sync Project install None (--no-install-project, run from src/) .venv changes only with dependencies Runtime copy .venv and src as separate layers A source edit invalidates only the src layer Import path PYTHONPATH=/app/src Package importable without an install Runtime user Fixed UID/GID 10001, no login shell Non-root, stable ownership, matches no host account

docs.title: Image Digest Resolution
docs.text: How one built image surfaces as different digests across Artifact Registry, CI, and Cloud Run — and how to verify provenance end to end.

docs.title: The Three Digests
docs.text:
A single docker buildx push from CI produces three content-addressed objects describing the image, plus a shared cache artifact (see The Registry Cache Artifact):

Object What it is Where you see it Image index (manifest list) The envelope buildx pushes. Contains pointers to the platform image and the attestation Registry tags ({sha}, latest, {version}), resolve-image-digest.yml output, Terraform docker_image, Cloud Run service spec Platform image manifest The actual runnable linux/amd64 image Cloud Run revision spec (spec.containers[0].image) Attestation manifest BuildKit provenance metadata (SLSA), platform unknown/unknown Inside the index only; annotated vnd.docker.reference.type: attestation-manifest

Two consequences follow:

  1. The index exists even for single-platform builds. Provenance attestations are added to images by default by buildx, and attestations are stored as manifest objects in the image index — so the OCI index wrapper appears around even a lone linux/amd64 image.
  2. The tag digest never matches the revision digest. Two documented behaviors compose here: Cloud Run resolves the deployed image to a digest the revision then always serves (deploying images: "If you deploy from a container image tag, it will be resolved to a digest and the revision will always serve this particular digest"), and container runtimes select the platform-matching image from an image index. The digest recorded on a revision is therefore the linux/amd64 child, not the index the tag names — confirm against your own service with the commands below. A mismatch between tag digest and revision digest is expected, not a deployment integrity problem.

Note

The Artifact Registry console may show a third "image" with platform unknown/unknown under the same upload. That is the attestation manifest, not a mis-built artifact — the attestation storage spec sets platform to unknown/unknown and annotates the manifest with vnd.docker.reference.digest pointing at the image it attests.

docs.title: The Registry Cache Artifact
docs.text:
The build workflow also pushes BuildKit layer cache to the same image name under the buildcache tag (cache-to: type=registry,...:buildcache,mode=max in docker-build.yml). This is an OCI image manifest holding cached layers for every build stage — mode=max includes intermediate builder-stage layers that never ship in the runtime image.

Properties that distinguish it from the image objects above:

  • Overwritten on every build (one buildcache tag per image name, not per commit)
  • Never deployed — Cloud Run never references it; it exists only for cache-from on subsequent builds
  • Why fully cached rebuilds reproduce byte-identical digests: a rerun on the same source pulls every layer from this cache, re-executes nothing, and exports the same manifests

When browsing the repository, expect it alongside the per-build objects.

docs.title: Resolving the Chain
docs.text:
Trace tag → index → platform image with these commands. Authenticate Docker once if needed:

gcloud auth configure-docker ${LOCATION}-docker.pkg.dev

1. Tag → index digest (what CI resolves and Terraform deploys):

gcloud artifacts docker images describe \
  "${LOCATION}-docker.pkg.dev/${PROJECT}/${REPO}/${IMAGE}:${TAG}" \
  --format "value(image_summary.digest)"

2. Index → children (platform image + attestation):

docker buildx imagetools inspect \
  "${LOCATION}-docker.pkg.dev/${PROJECT}/${REPO}/${IMAGE}@${INDEX_DIGEST}"

The output lists the linux/amd64 manifest digest and an unknown/unknown attestation manifest whose vnd.docker.reference.digest annotation points back at the platform image.

3. Cloud Run service → deployed index digest:

gcloud run services describe ${SERVICE} --region ${LOCATION} \
  --format "value(spec.template.spec.containers[0].image)"

4. Cloud Run revision → running platform digest:

gcloud run revisions describe ${REVISION} --region ${LOCATION} \
  --format "value(spec.containers[0].image)"

5. CI build log → both digests at export time (proves what a workflow run produced):

gh run view ${RUN_ID} --log | grep -E "exporting manifest|exporting manifest list|pushing manifest"

Look for exporting manifest sha256:... (platform image) followed by exporting manifest list sha256:... (index). A rerun whose layers all report CACHED reproduces both digests byte-identically.

Tip

The repo also bundles this procedure as the verify-image-provenance agent skill, usable with your AI coding assistant of choice.

docs.title: Console Paths
docs.text:
• Artifact Registry: Console → Artifact Registry → Repositories → {agent_name}-{env} → image name. The digest list shows the index (carries the tags) and its children. Click a digest → Manifest tab for the raw JSON.
  • Cloud Run service (deployed index): Console → Cloud Run → service → Revisions tab → "Image URL" column header area shows the service-level image; YAML view shows spec.template.spec.containers[0].image.
  • Cloud Run revision (running platform image): Console → Cloud Run → service → Revisions tab → select revision → Containers section → "Image" shows the digest-qualified URI Cloud Run recorded at import.
  • Build provenance: GitHub → Actions → CI/CD Pipeline run → Build Docker Image job → "Build and Push to Artifact Registry" step log.

docs.title: Worked Example
docs.text:
From the v0.16.0 release (commit 4ae72ab):

Tags 4ae72ab, latest, v0.16.0
  → index sha256:87d5625f...          (what resolve-image-digest passed to Terraform)
      ├── linux/amd64 manifest sha256:5cc32590...   (what revisions record)
      └── attestation manifest sha256:95cb7bf4...   (provenance for 5cc32590)

Revisions 00065 and 00066 both record 5cc32590... — two deploy attempts of the same index resolve to the same platform image. During the incident that motivated this doc, that equality is what proved a startup failure was transient infrastructure rather than a bad build: the byte-identical image failed its startup probe once and served cleanly on the rerun.

docs.title: Debugging With Digests
docs.text:
• "The revision digest doesn't match what CI deployed" — expected; compare the revision digest against the index's linux/amd64 child (step 2 above), not against the tag.
  • "Did the rerun deploy the same image?" — compare spec.containers[0].image across the two revisions. Revision image fields are immutable, so equality is proof. Corroborate with the build log: all-CACHED layers reproduce identical digests.
  • "Which commit produced the running image?" — find the running revision's platform digest, locate its parent index (docker buildx imagetools inspect on each tagged index, or the Artifact Registry console child view), and read the index's {sha} tag.
  • "Is this unknown/unknown artifact a problem?" — no; it is the provenance attestation. It never runs.

docs.title: Integration Tests
docs.text: The integration lane: the real FastAPI app exercised against a real Postgres session service.

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
The integration lane (tests/integration/) exercises the real FastAPI app against a real Postgres session service with no mocks. It builds the production app via ADK get_fast_api_app() with a postgresql+asyncpg:// URI (a real DatabaseSessionService) and drives it in-process with httpx ASGITransport. The only substitution is the LLM: root_agent.model is replaced with a deterministic stub, so the run path persists and reads session state without a network call or cost.

The lane is deterministic and runs only by explicit path (uv run pytest tests/integration); it never calls the live model.

docs.title: What it covers
docs.text:
• Session lifecycle through the API: create, get, list, delete
  • An agent run that persists events and reads back session state
  • Postgres dialect strictness: asyncpg rejects ISO strings for timestamptz where sqlite tolerates them, so direct SQL binds native Python objects via typed bindparam. These tests demonstrate the asyncpg strictness constraint that motivates the typed-bindparam convention in AGENTS.md; the session-lifecycle and agent-run tests are what actually catch dialect regressions through DatabaseSessionService.

docs.title: Run it locally
docs.text:
The lane starts its own Postgres, so a running Docker daemon is the only prerequisite:

uv run pytest tests/integration

Any Docker daemon the docker CLI reaches through its active context works without extra setup, including one whose socket is not at /var/run/docker.sock. The lane's conftest.py runs docker info first, so an unreachable daemon fails the run immediately, then points testcontainers at the active context's socket and disables its Ryuk cleanup container, which cannot mount a socket that exists only on the host. A DOCKER_HOST you set yourself takes precedence, and the hook leaves Ryuk enabled in that case. Without Ryuk, a run killed before teardown can leave its Postgres container behind; list leftovers with docker ps -a --filter label=org.testcontainers=true.

The database_uri fixture starts a throwaway Postgres container via testcontainers (image pinned by POSTGRES_IMAGE in the test module) and tears it down at session end. To point the lane at an already-running Postgres instead (and skip the container), set INTEGRATION_DATABASE_URI. The conftest's Docker setup is skipped too, so no Docker daemon is needed:

INTEGRATION_DATABASE_URI=postgresql+asyncpg://postgres:postgres@127.0.0.1:5432/sessions \
  uv run pytest tests/integration

This is a test-harness variable, not application runtime config, so it lives here rather than in docs/environment-variables.md.

Note

The lane needs no GCP credentials. An autouse session fixture (_mock_gcp_credentials) in the test module patches dotenv.load_dotenv and google.auth.default. A fixture suffices because the lane imports the source package lazily — inside integration_app, after collection — so the patch lands before any agent code runs.

docs.title: How CI provides Postgres
docs.text:
The ci.yml integration job needs no service container: testcontainers starts a throwaway Postgres on the runner's Docker daemon (present on ubuntu-latest), the same path a developer runs locally. The major version tracks the deployed Cloud SQL instance (POSTGRES_18 in terraform/main/database.tf), so the lane exercises the dialect production actually runs, and pinning the image in one place (POSTGRES_IMAGE in the test module) keeps the CI workflow and the lane from drifting on the version. The job is gated on the changes job and folded into the always-runs status sentinel, so the single required check CI / status covers it. It runs uv run pytest tests/integration without --cov — the 100% coverage gate is unit-lane-only.

docs.title: Manual Environment Protection
docs.text:
Configure the prod-apply approval gate by hand in the GitHub UI or with gh api, for repositories whose environments bootstrap does not manage.

Bootstrap configures environment protection from terraform/bootstrap/prod/terraform.tfvars and terraform/bootstrap/stage/main.tf (Protection Strategies). Use this page when you set protection on an environment outside that root, or when you need the raw API calls to inspect or repair a setting.

Warning

In a repository where terraform/bootstrap/prod and terraform/bootstrap/stage manage the environments, every bootstrap apply reverts settings made here to the values in those roots. Make lasting changes there, or the next apply undoes them.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
Setting Recommended Why Required reviewers The users or teams who own production releases (up to six; one approval releases the job) The approval gate itself Prevent self-review On for a team; off for a solo maintainer Stops the person who pushed the promotion tag from approving their own deployment. A solo maintainer who turns it on can never approve Wait timer Off, unless you want a cooling-off window Delays the job after approval is requested Allow administrators to bypass Off for strict release control; on to keep a break-glass path An admin can deploy without an approval Deployment branches and tags Selected branches and tags, with tag rule prod-v*.*.* Prod jobs only run on promotion tag pushes, so GitHub checks the rule against a refs/tags/... ref. Leave out a main branch rule: it never matches a prod run, and it would let any future job that targets the environment on a main push deploy

Apply the same tag rule to the prod environment, which prod-promote, prod-plan and prod-smoke target, so a tag outside the promotion format cannot reach prod credentials through those jobs. Give the stage environment a main branch rule and the same tag rule: stage jobs run on pushes to main, and promotion runs read the stage registry under stage. Each environment's WIF provider trusts only its environments' tokens, so these rules decide which refs can reach the stage and prod projects.

docs.title: Configure in the GitHub UI
docs.text:
1. Go to Settings → Environments → prod-apply
  2. Under Deployment protection rules:
  3. Check Required reviewers and add users or teams
  4. Set Prevent self-review per the table above
  5. Optionally set Wait timer
  6. Set Allow administrators to bypass per the table above
  7. Click Save protection rules
  8. Under Deployment branches and tags, select Selected branches and tags and add a tag rule prod-v*.*.*
  9. Click Save protection rules
  10. Repeat step 4 for the prod environment
  11. For the stage environment, select Selected branches and tags, add a branch rule main and a tag rule prod-v*.*.*, and save

docs.title: Configure with gh api
docs.text:
The environments REST API sets the protection rules in one PUT, and the deployment branch policies API adds the tag rule.

Warning

The PUT replaces the environment's reviewers, self-review setting and wait timer with the body's values. Include every reviewer you want to keep, or they are removed.

# Look up the reviewer's numeric ID (a team: gh api orgs/<org>/teams/<team-slug> --jq .id)
REVIEWER_ID=$(gh api users/<github-login> --jq .id)

# Reviewers, self-review, wait timer, and a custom branch/tag policy.
# prevent_self_review is false for a solo maintainer; set it to true for a team
gh api --method PUT repos/:owner/:repo/environments/prod-apply --input - <<EOF
{
  "reviewers": [{"type": "User", "id": ${REVIEWER_ID}}],
  "prevent_self_review": false,
  "wait_timer": 0,
  "deployment_branch_policy": {"protected_branches": false, "custom_branch_policies": true}
}
EOF

# Allow only promotion tags to deploy
gh api --method POST repos/:owner/:repo/environments/prod-apply/deployment-branch-policies \
  -f name='prod-v*.*.*' -f type=tag

The PUT body has no admin-bypass field: set Allow administrators to bypass in the UI.

To replace an existing tag rule, list the rules, delete the old one by ID, then add the new one:

gh api repos/:owner/:repo/environments/prod-apply/deployment-branch-policies \
  --jq '.branch_policies[] | {id, name, type}'
gh api --method DELETE repos/:owner/:repo/environments/prod-apply/deployment-branch-policies/<policy-id>
gh api --method POST repos/:owner/:repo/environments/prod-apply/deployment-branch-policies \
  -f name='prod-v*.*.*' -f type=tag

For the prod environment, the same calls apply with prod in place of prod-apply; send only deployment_branch_policy in its PUT body. For stage, send the same deployment_branch_policy body, add the same tag rule, and add a branch rule:

gh api --method POST repos/:owner/:repo/environments/stage/deployment-branch-policies \
  -f name='main' -f type=branch

docs.title: Verify
docs.text:
GitHub UI: Settings → Environments → prod-apply shows the reviewers, the self-review and bypass settings, and the prod-v*.*.* tag rule under Deployment branches and tags.

CLI: 

gh api repos/:owner/:repo/environments/prod-apply --jq '{
  reviewers: [.protection_rules[] | select(.type == "required_reviewers") | .reviewers[] | {type, login: (.reviewer.login // .reviewer.slug)}],
  prevent_self_review: (.protection_rules[] | select(.type == "required_reviewers") | .prevent_self_review),
  wait_timer: ([.protection_rules[] | select(.type == "wait_timer") | .wait_timer][0] // 0),
  can_admins_bypass,
  deployment_branch_policy
}'
gh api repos/:owner/:repo/environments/prod-apply/deployment-branch-policies \
  --jq '[.branch_policies[] | {name, type}]'

Expected: a non-empty reviewers list, custom_branch_policies: true, and a {"name": "prod-v*.*.*", "type": "tag"} policy.

Plan availability for private repositories is in Protection Strategies.
