docs.title: OpenTelemetry Architecture
docs.text: Provider ownership, the ADK telemetry patch, export to Google Cloud, the resource, and dependency decisions for telemetry.py.

docs.title: Provider Ownership
docs.text:
The application owns all three OpenTelemetry providers. server.py runs, at import time:

env = initialize_environment()  # ServerEnv
# Tracer, logger and (with cloud.region) meter providers set globally
configure_telemetry(...)
app = get_fast_api_app(...)  # ADK attaches only its web UI processors

configure_telemetry() builds one resource and the providers that share it, then sets them globally: a TracerProvider with the template's sampler (see Trace Context and Sampling) and a BatchSpanProcessor, a LoggerProvider with a BatchLogRecordProcessor always, and a MeterProvider with a PeriodicExportingMetricReader (default 60 second interval) only when the resource has cloud.region (see Export). The meter provider gets its own resource: the shared one without the cloud_run_revision attributes. It also attaches the OTel logging handler to the root logger through LoggingInstrumentor (trace context on every record). A filter on the uvicorn.access logger drops /health access lines (Cloud Run probes), so they reach neither stdout nor Cloud Logging; it is a logger filter because uvicorn's logging config replaces handlers but keeps filters.

It must run before get_fast_api_app(): the patched ADK setup raises RuntimeError when the providers are not set yet.

docs.title: The ADK Telemetry Patch
docs.text:
get_fast_api_app() calls ADK's private google.adk.cli.api_server._setup_telemetry(), passing the web UI's processors: ApiServerSpanExporter and InMemoryExporter for spans, and WebUiLogExporter for the GenAI event records that show message content in the trace view. Unpatched, that function:

  • Builds its own providers with OTLP/HTTP exporters when any OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_* endpoint is set, and instruments the GenAI SDK. With the application's providers already set, its set_*_provider calls do nothing, and the web UI processors passed in the same call are dropped
  • Never attaches log processors to a logger provider set elsewhere, on any path

telemetry.py replaces it at import with _attach_web_ui_processors(), which adds the web UI's span and log processors to the global providers and does nothing else. ADK then builds no providers, exporters or instrumentation of its own, whatever OTLP variables are set. With the web UI off, ADK passes no processors and the function returns.

The patch follows ADK's own direction: google/adk-python#3548 made the default path reuse an initialized tracer provider. It is removable once an ADK release attaches the processors to already-set providers on every path. tests/unit/test_telemetry.py asserts it is applied.

docs.title: Export
docs.text:
Every signal exports to the Google Cloud Telemetry API (TELEMETRY_API_ENDPOINT in telemetry.py, https://telemetry.googleapis.com:443) over TLS channel credentials carrying Application Default Credentials (cloud-platform scope). Telemetry targets Google Cloud only; to use another backend, replace telemetry.py.

configure_telemetry() passes the endpoint to every exporter explicitly, so the SDK's OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_* endpoint variables and its localhost:4317 default never apply. The SDK still reads the other OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_* variables itself: headers, certificates, compression and timeout. At startup it prints the endpoint, whether metrics are on for the run, and the exported resource attributes.

Metrics on Google: the Telemetry API rejects metric points without a location, so metrics go there only when the meter resource has cloud.region. On Cloud Run the GCP resource detector supplies it from the metadata server, so metrics flow automatically. Locally, add cloud.region=<region> to OTEL_RESOURCE_ATTRIBUTES to send them to Google. Without a region, no meter provider is set, so ADK's metric calls do nothing. Metrics land in Cloud Monitoring as prometheus.googleapis.com/<name>/<kind> on the prometheus_target resource, beside Cloud Run's native run.googleapis.com metrics, which the alert policies read.

The standard OTEL_SDK_DISABLED=true turns export off: the SDK providers read it themselves and hand out no-op tracers, loggers and meters, so nothing is recorded or exported and the web UI trace view stays empty. configure_telemetry() does not read it, so startup still looks up Application Default Credentials and prints the usual lines.

Export timing on Cloud Run: every signal exports from background batch processors (spans and logs every few seconds, metrics every 60 seconds). The service allocates CPU only while it handles requests (cpu_idle = true in terraform/main/main.tf), so after a request ends the export threads barely run, and that request's traces, logs and metrics can reach Google only when a later request gives the instance CPU again. On a busy service the delay is short; on a quiet one it can be minutes. Two ways to remove it, neither applied by the template:

  • Flush at the end of each request: middleware that calls force_flush() on the tracer and logger providers before the response completes. Costs a little latency per request, no extra billing.
  • Keep CPU allocated between requests: cpu_idle = false. Exports run on schedule, and the service moves to instance-based billing for CPU.

Only server.py (uv run server and the container entry point) runs this setup. adk web, adk api_server and adk run build their app through ADK's own telemetry setup.

Telemetry API permissions for the runtime service account: roles/telemetry.tracesWriter (traces), roles/logging.logWriter (logs) and roles/telemetry.metricsWriter (metrics), all in app_iam_roles in terraform/main/main.tf.

docs.title: Trace Context and Sampling
docs.text:
ADK's get_fast_api_app() runs a middleware on every request that continues the caller's trace: when the request carries a W3C traceparent header and GOOGLE_CLOUD_AGENT_ENGINE_ID is unset, ADK makes that header's span the parent of its invoke_workflow span (since ADK 2.14.0, google/adk-python#7846). Without the header, invoke_workflow starts a new trace.

Cloud Run adds a traceparent to every request but marks only some of them sampled: it samples at most 0.1 requests per second per instance, a rate cap rather than a percentage, so each instance sends at most one sampled request every 10 seconds and the rest arrive unsampled. The SDK's default sampler, ParentBased(ALWAYS_ON), follows a remote parent's sampled flag. Under it, an agent turn is recorded only when it happens to be the request Cloud Run sampled, and every other turn's spans are dropped. Which turns survive depends on arrival order, since health checks and session calls compete for the same slot, and the share kept shrinks as traffic grows (about 1% at 10 requests per second on one instance). build_sampler() returns ParentBased(root=ALWAYS_ON, remote_parent_not_sampled=ALWAYS_ON) instead:

  • Every agent request is traced, whatever Cloud Run sampled
  • ADK's spans keep the caller's trace ID, so on Cloud Run the request log entry, the application logs and the agent spans share one trace ID. Cloud Run stores its own span for the request only when it sampled it
  • A caller that sends its own traceparent, like another instrumented service, gets the agent spans inside its trace

Recording every turn suits development and low-volume services. Span volume, cost and noise grow with traffic, so a high-volume service should sample by ratio instead. Setting the standard OTEL_TRACES_SAMPLER replaces this sampler: build_sampler() returns None and the SDK reads the variable. Pick a sampler that ignores the parent's flag, like traceidratio with OTEL_TRACES_SAMPLER_ARG=0.1 to keep a tenth of agent turns regardless of what Cloud Run sampled. A parent-based value, like parentbased_always_on (the SDK default), brings back Cloud Run's rate cap described above. Every recorded span counts toward Cloud Trace pricing; Cloud Run's own spans are free.

docs.title: Resource
docs.text:
build_resources() merges, lowest precedence first:

  1. The SDK defaults (telemetry.sdk.*)
  2. The GCP resource detector (opentelemetry-resourcedetector-gcp): cloud.* and faas.* attributes on Cloud Run, nothing locally
  3. The template's values: service.name (AGENT_NAME), service.instance.id, gcp.project_id (GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT)
  4. The environment's OTEL_SERVICE_NAME and OTEL_RESOURCE_ATTRIBUTES

The result is the meter resource. When the detector reports cloud.platform=gcp_cloud_run, the traces and logs resource adds the cloud_run_revision attributes mapped from the detected ones (see Log Placement); elsewhere both are the same resource. The Telemetry API rejects logs whose resource lacks gcp.project_id.

docs.title: Log Placement
docs.text:
Log names: the Telemetry API names a log after a record's event_name, or otlp when it has none. Application logs land in otlp and GenAI events in gen_ai.client.inference.operation.details. Filter by service through the resource labels.

Resource type: the Telemetry API maps OTLP logs to generic_task unless the resource names a monitored resource. On Cloud Run, the traces and logs resource carries gcp.resource_type=cloud_run_revision with project_id, service_name (faas.name), revision_name (faas.version), configuration_name (K_CONFIGURATION, which the detector reads but does not export) and location (cloud.region), so the logs appear in the service's Logs tab beside stdout. Locally the detector reports nothing, so logs stay on generic_task; service.namespace in OTEL_RESOURCE_ATTRIBUTES tells developers apart. ADK uses the same mechanism to place Agent Engine logs. Traces carry the attributes too. The meter resource leaves them off, because the Telemetry API drops metric points that carry gcp.resource_type; it keeps cloud.region from the detector or OTEL_RESOURCE_ATTRIBUTES, which wins.

SDK diagnostics: the opentelemetry logger writes to the console with propagation off, so an export failure is printed rather than handed back to the log exporter that is failing.

docs.title: GenAI Instrumentation
docs.text:
ADK records the model call span (generate_content {model}), the GenAI event log records, token usage and its GenAI metrics itself. The template does not install GoogleGenAiSdkInstrumentor: ADK hands it the inference span only under OTEL_SEMCONV_STABILITY_OPT_IN=gen_ai_latest_experimental, and with that opt-in and content capture on, the instrumentor fails to serialize a Pydantic tool response such as load_memory's.

The template does not set OTEL_SEMCONV_STABILITY_OPT_IN. ADK's default telemetry schema already emits the experimental GenAI semantic conventions, and the opt-in only routes the inference span to the GenAI SDK instrumentor, which the template does not install.

Message content placement is ADK's: OTEL_INSTRUMENTATION_GENAI_CAPTURE_MESSAGE_CONTENT selects events, spans or both (Message Content Capture).

docs.title: ADK Span Hierarchy
docs.text:
ADK produces its own span hierarchy using the gcp.vertex.agent tracer. The names below are ADK's default telemetry schema (OpenTelemetry GenAI semconv v2); setting ADK_TELEMETRY_SCHEMA_VERSION_OPT_IN=otel_semconv_1_36 restores the legacy schema, which names the top-level span invocation and wraps each model call in a call_llm span:

Span Name Purpose invoke_workflow Top-level span for a runner invocation invoke_agent {name} Agent-level span with agent name, session ID generate_content {model} Model inference execute_tool {name} Individual tool execution

docs.title: ADK Metrics
docs.text: ADK records into the global MeterProvider (meter gcp.vertex.agent) whenever one is set. Seven gen_ai.* histograms are on by default: operation duration, token usage (gen_ai.client.token.usage, input and output), agent, workflow and tool durations, and per-agent inference and tool call counts. ADK_EXPERIMENTAL_TELEMETRY=TRUE, which the template sets locally (.env.example) and on Cloud Run, adds the adk.experimental.* set: per-agent and per-workflow token breakdowns (cache reads, reasoning, tool input), workflow call counts, skill loads and compactions, plus experimental span attributes such as context-cache and grounding data. ADK_EXPERIMENTAL_TELEMETRY_FEATURES selects individual features instead.

docs.title: Direct Dependencies
docs.text: Package Purpose opentelemetry-exporter-otlp-proto-grpc OTLP gRPC exporters for all three signals opentelemetry-instrumentation-logging Attaches the OTel handler to the root logger and adds trace context to LogRecords opentelemetry-resourcedetector-gcp Cloud Run resource attributes, including the region the log placement needs

docs.title: Transitive Dependencies (via ADK)
docs.text: opentelemetry-api and opentelemetry-sdk come from ADK, which caps their version; the OTLP exporter and contrib instrumentations follow that cap. ADK's [gcp] and [otel-gcp] extras also install packages the template does not import, like the GCP-native trace, logging and monitoring exporters and the GenAI SDK instrumentor.

docs.title: Background Task Context Propagation
docs.text:
FastAPI BackgroundTasks (via Starlette) does not propagate Python's contextvars across the async boundary. Any OpenTelemetry spans started in a background task are orphaned from the parent trace unless the OTel context is manually forwarded.

Pattern:

from opentelemetry import context as otel_context

# In the request handler — capture context before scheduling
current_ctx = otel_context.get_current()
background_tasks.add_task(my_background_fn, ..., parent_otel_context=current_ctx)

# In the background function — attach and detach in try/finally
async def my_background_fn(..., parent_otel_context=None):
    token = (
        otel_context.attach(parent_otel_context)
        if parent_otel_context is not None
        else None
    )
    try:
        with tracer.start_as_current_span("my_span"):
            ...  # spans are linked to the parent trace
    finally:
        if token is not None:
            otel_context.detach(token)

Both attach() and detach() execute inside the background task's own async contextvars.Context. Because the token is created and released in the same context, no ValueError is raised and no defensive suppression is needed. This invariant is load-bearing: any refactor that moves otel_context.attach(...) outside the background task (e.g., back into the sync request handler) will introduce the "Token was created in a different Context" class of error.

← Back to References | Documentation

docs.title: Protection Strategies Reference
docs.text: Branch, tag, and environment protection setup and rationale.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Three protection layers ensure code quality and security:

  1. Branch Protection (main) - Manual setup, requires PR approval and status checks
  2. Tag Protection (prod-v*) - Automated by bootstrap (production mode), limits prod promotion to admins
  3. Environment Protection (prod, prod-apply) - Automated by bootstrap from terraform.tfvars, approval gate for production

docs.title: Branch Protection (Manual Setup Required)
docs.text: Main branch protection ensures code quality and prevents accidental commits to main.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Repository admin access — only admins (or org owners) can configure branch protection rules.
  • Status check names must already exist before you can require them. GitHub's required-status-check picker only offers check names it has seen at least once on the repository. If a workflow has never run, the check it produces won't appear as a selectable option. Three common paths:
  • Existing repo: the workflow is already on main and has run on prior pushes — the status check name is already in the picker.
  • Fresh repo: open a PR that adds .github/workflows/ci.yml. Workflows triggered by pull_request events run from the PR head ref (not the target branch), so the workflow runs on the PR even before protection is configured. After the first run completes, the status check name appears in the picker. Configure protection, then merge the PR.
  • Migrating an existing repo to a renamed required check (like the Required Checks / required-status → CI / status rename): open a PR with the new/renamed workflow. After the first run on the PR, edit the protection rule to add the new check name and remove the old one before merging. Doing the swap on the PR (rather than after merge) avoids a window where the rule references a check that no longer exists.

docs.title: What to Configure
docs.text:
1. Require pull request before merging:
  2. Require approvals: 1 (minimum)

  3. Dismiss stale reviews when new commits are pushed: ✅

  4. Require status checks to pass:

  5. Require branches to be up to date: ✅

  6. Status checks required:

    • CI / status (from .github/workflows/ci.yml)

  7. Do not allow bypassing settings:

  8. Allow specific actors to bypass: Repository admins only

  9. Other settings:

  10. ❌ Require linear history (optional, not required)
  11. ❌ Allow force pushes (keep disabled)
  12. ❌ Allow deletions (keep disabled)

docs.title: How to Configure (GitHub UI)
docs.text:
1. Go to repository Settings → Branches
  2. Click Add branch protection rule
  3. Enter branch name pattern: main
  4. Configure protection settings:
  5. ✅ Require a pull request before merging
    • Required approvals: 1
    • ✅ Dismiss stale pull request approvals when new commits are pushed
  6. ✅ Require status checks to pass before merging
    • ✅ Require branches to be up to date before merging
    • Search for and select: CI / status
  7. ✅ Do not allow bypassing the above settings
    • Allow specific actors to bypass: Repository admins (optional)
  8. ❌ Require linear history (optional)
  9. ❌ Allow force pushes (disabled)
  10. ❌ Allow deletions (disabled)
  11. Click Create or Save changes

docs.title: Verify
docs.text:
GitHub UI: 1. Settings → Branches 2. Confirm main branch protection rule exists 3. Check rule shows: 1 required approval, required status checks, dismiss stale reviews

CLI: 

gh api repos/:owner/:repo/branches/main/protection | jq '{
  pr_reviews: .required_pull_request_reviews.required_approving_review_count,
  dismiss_stale: .required_pull_request_reviews.dismiss_stale_reviews,
  status_checks: .required_status_checks.contexts
}'

docs.title: Why Manual?
docs.text:
Branch protection rules are repository-wide policy decisions that vary by team workflow. Terraform would override manual adjustments on every apply.

Different teams may want: - Different approval counts (1 vs 2) - Different required status checks - Different bypass permissions - CODEOWNERS enforcement

Bootstrap can't predict these preferences, so we make it a manual configuration step.

docs.title: Tag Protection (Automated)
docs.text: Production tag protection is automatically configured by bootstrap in production mode.

docs.title: What Bootstrap Creates
docs.text:
A release is two tags on one commit: vX.Y.Z marks the release and deploys nothing, and prod-vX.Y.Z promotes it to prod. Bootstrap (terraform/bootstrap/prod/) creates the Production Promotion Tag Protection ruleset on refs/tags/prod-v*: only repository admins can create, move or delete a promotion tag, so only an admin can start the template's prod promotion pipeline. v* release tags have no ruleset, since pushing one deploys nothing.

Note

The ruleset also guards prod credentials. The prod Workload Identity Federation provider accepts only tokens from the prod and prod-apply environments, which accept only prod-v*.*.* tags (Environment Protection).

docs.title: Verify
docs.text:
GitHub UI: 1. Settings → Rules → Rulesets 2. Confirm the ruleset exists: Production Promotion Tag Protection 3. Check details: - Enforcement: Active - Target: Tags - Patterns: refs/tags/prod-v*

CLI: 

gh api repos/:owner/:repo/rulesets | jq '.[] | {name, enforcement, target}'

Expected output: 

{
  "name": "Production Promotion Tag Protection",
  "enforcement": "active",
  "target": "tag"
}

docs.title: Why Automated?
docs.text:
Tag protection is environment-specific infrastructure: - Production mode requires tag protection (prod-v* tags trigger prod deployments) - Dev-only mode doesn't need tag protection (no tag starts a deployment)

Bootstrap enforces this consistently based on deployment mode. No manual decision needed.

docs.title: Environment Protection (Automated)
docs.text: Bootstrap creates and configures the prod and prod-apply GitHub Environments from terraform/bootstrap/prod/terraform.tfvars, and the stage environment's deployment rules from terraform/bootstrap/stage/main.tf. Every bootstrap apply enforces those values, so change protection there and re-apply; a change made in the GitHub UI is reverted by the next apply of that root. To set protection by hand outside bootstrap, see Manual Environment Protection.

docs.title: What Bootstrap Configures
docs.text:
Setting Environment Source Recommended Deployment tag rule prod-v*.*.* prod, prod-apply Fixed in the prod root Not configurable: the prod jobs only run on promotion tag pushes, so only a prod-v*.*.* tag can use either environment Deployment branch rule main, tag rule prod-v*.*.* stage Fixed in the stage root Not configurable: the stage jobs run on pushes to main, and a promotion run reads the stage registry under stage Required reviewers prod-apply prod_apply_reviewer_users (GitHub logins), prod_apply_reviewer_teams (team slugs) The users or teams who own production releases (up to six; one approval releases the job) Prevent self-review prod-apply prod_apply_prevent_self_review On for a team; off for a solo maintainer, who could otherwise never approve Allow administrators to bypass prod-apply prod_apply_can_admins_bypass Off for strict release control; on to keep a break-glass path Wait timer prod-apply prod_apply_wait_timer (minutes) Off (null), unless you want a cooling-off window

The tag rule matches the promotion tag format the tag ruleset limits to admins, so only an admin-pushed promotion tag reaches the approval. The rules also limit credentials: each environment's WIF provider accepts only tokens from its own GitHub Environments, so a ref these rules reject cannot authenticate to the stage or prod project (Security Posture Identity Layer). terraform.tfvars.example sets a starting value for each variable; replace the placeholder reviewer with your own.

docs.title: Verify
docs.text:
GitHub UI: Settings → Environments → prod-apply shows the reviewers, the self-review and bypass settings, and the prod-v*.*.* tag rule under Deployment branches and tags. prod shows the same tag rule, and stage shows a main branch rule plus the same tag rule.

CLI: 

gh api repos/:owner/:repo/environments/prod-apply --jq '{
  reviewers: [.protection_rules[] | select(.type == "required_reviewers") | .reviewers[] | {type, login: (.reviewer.login // .reviewer.slug)}],
  prevent_self_review: (.protection_rules[] | select(.type == "required_reviewers") | .prevent_self_review),
  wait_timer: ([.protection_rules[] | select(.type == "wait_timer") | .wait_timer][0] // 0),
  can_admins_bypass,
  deployment_branch_policy
}'
for env in stage prod prod-apply; do
  gh api repos/:owner/:repo/environments/$env/deployment-branch-policies --jq '[.branch_policies[] | {name, type}]'
done

Expected: the reviewers from terraform.tfvars, custom_branch_policies: true, and exactly one {"name": "prod-v*.*.*", "type": "tag"} policy per environment, plus {"name": "main", "type": "branch"} on stage. A second policy (like an older v*.*.* rule created by hand) is not managed by bootstrap and keeps allowing those tags; delete it (set env to the environment that has it):

env=prod-apply
gh api repos/:owner/:repo/environments/$env/deployment-branch-policies \
  --jq '.branch_policies[] | {id, name, type}'
gh api --method DELETE repos/:owner/:repo/environments/$env/deployment-branch-policies/<policy-id>

docs.title: Private Repositories
docs.text:
GitHub gates environment protection by plan for private repositories (deployments and environments):

Repository Required reviewers, wait timer, admin bypass Deployment branch and tag policy Public, any plan Available Available Private, GitHub Free Not available Not available Private, GitHub Pro or Team Not available Available Private, GitHub Enterprise Available Available

On a private repository without GitHub Enterprise, leave prod_apply_reviewer_users and prod_apply_reviewer_teams empty.

Warning

On a private repository without GitHub Enterprise there is no approval gate: prod-apply deploys to production as soon as prod-plan finishes, with no reviewer prompt.

What still guards production on those plans:

  • require-stage-success. prod-promote needs it, so a promotion tag deploys only a commit whose merge run passed Apply Stage, Smoke Stage, and Judge Eval. This holds on every plan because it is a job dependency, not an environment rule.
  • The deployment branch and tag policy (Pro and Team only). Only prod-v*.*.* tags reach prod and prod-apply, and only main and those tags reach stage. On GitHub Free, a workflow on any branch can declare environment: stage or environment: prod and receive that project's credentials.
  • Who can push a prod-v* tag. The promotion tag ruleset limits this to admins where your plan enforces rulesets on private repositories; confirm it shows Active under Settings → Rules → Rulesets. Without it, anyone with write access can start the prod promotion pipeline.

To keep a human approval on a private fork, use GitHub Enterprise or make the repository public.

docs.title: Production Deployment Flow
docs.text:
1. A release tag (vX.Y.Z) marks the commit and deploys nothing
  2. After that commit's merge run passes its stage jobs, a repository admin pushes the promotion tag (prod-vX.Y.Z) on the same commit. Commands: Release a Version: Promote to Production
  3. GitHub Actions workflow starts. Metadata extraction fails unless the promotion tag has the form prod-vX.Y.Z and vX.Y.Z marks the same commit, and the tag must match the prod-v*.*.* tag rule to reach prod and prod-apply
  4. Jobs run sequentially:
  5. Resolve image digest from stage
  6. Promote image to prod registry
  7. Run Terraform plan for prod
  8. prod-apply job waits for approval (requires prod-apply Environment configured reviewer from approved list)
  9. Configured reviewer sees notification: "Review deployments waiting"
  10. Reviewer checks:
  11. Deployment logs and outputs
  12. Plan changes
  13. Staging environment validation
  14. Reviewer approves or rejects
  15. If approved: Terraform apply runs, deploys to production
  16. If rejected: Workflow fails, no deployment

Note

A tag that doesn't match the prod-v*.*.* tag rule is blocked by the environment before the approval prompt.

docs.title: Approving a Deployment
docs.text:
GitHub UI: 1. Go to Actions tab 2. Click on the waiting workflow run 3. Click Review deployments button 4. Select environment: prod-apply 5. Add comment (optional but recommended): "LGTM - staging validation passed" 6. Click Approve and deploy or Reject

CLI: gh has no approval subcommand, but the pending deployments API approves as any required reviewer:

# Find the waiting run
gh run list --workflow=ci-cd.yml --status waiting

# Show what it is waiting on
gh api repos/:owner/:repo/actions/runs/<run-id>/pending_deployments \
  --jq '.[] | {environment: .environment.name, id: .environment.id}'

# Approve (or "rejected")
ENV_ID=$(gh api repos/:owner/:repo/environments/prod-apply --jq .id)
gh api --method POST repos/:owner/:repo/actions/runs/<run-id>/pending_deployments \
  -F "environment_ids[]=${ENV_ID}" -f state=approved -f comment="Stage validation passed"

docs.title: Protection Strategy Summary
docs.text:
Protection Type When Why Branch (main) Manual After repo creation Team-specific workflow preferences Tags (prod-v*) Automated Bootstrap (prod mode) Environment-specific requirement Environments (prod, prod-apply) Automated Bootstrap (prod mode), from terraform.tfvars Reviewers are a human decision recorded in code and enforced on every apply

docs.title: Security Posture
docs.text: Rationale behind key security decisions, organized by defense layer. Each section explains why a choice was made and points to the authoritative source — the focused guides and Terraform files that implement and maintain the details.

docs.title: Defense-in-Depth Model
docs.text:
The project enforces security at every layer of the stack, from network topology down to application code. No single layer is relied upon alone — each compensates for potential weaknesses in the others.

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  Network           VPC, private IP, IAP, firewalls  │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  Identity          WIF, IAM database auth, no keys  │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  Database          Private-only, enforced proxy/TLS │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  Compute           COS bastion, Cloud Run Gen2      │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  Container         Non-root, multi-stage, pinned    │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  Storage           Public access prevention, UBLA   │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  Application       CORS validation, Pydantic, ruff  │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

docs.title: Network Layer
docs.text:
Private IP only, no public database endpoint. Cloud SQL has ipv4_enabled = false — the instance is unreachable from the public internet. All database traffic stays within the VPC via Private Services Access peering. This eliminates the largest attack surface (a publicly routable database) entirely, rather than relying on allowlists or firewall rules that can be misconfigured.

IAP-gated access, no SSH keys or VPN. The bastion has no public IP. All access routes through Identity-Aware Proxy, which authenticates via Google identity before any TCP connection is established. Firewall rules restrict the bastion's inbound traffic to Google's IAP CIDR range (35.235.240.0/20) on only ports 22 (SSH) and 5432 (proxy). This means a compromised bastion IP is useless without a valid Google identity — there is no network path to reach it otherwise.

Direct VPC egress from Cloud Run. Cloud Run uses PRIVATE_RANGES_ONLY egress to reach Cloud SQL through the VPC, avoiding a Serverless VPC Access connector (which adds cost and another component to secure).

  • Source: terraform/main/network.tf (VPC, firewall rules, Private Services Access)
  • Source: terraform/main/main.tf (Cloud Run VPC egress)
  • GCP docs: Private Services Access, IAP TCP forwarding, Direct VPC egress
  • Guide: Infrastructure

docs.title: Identity Layer
docs.text:
Workload Identity Federation (WIF), no service account keys. CI/CD authenticates to GCP using GitHub's OIDC tokens federated through WIF. No long-lived credentials exist — there are no JSON key files to leak, rotate, or revoke. The identity trust chain is: GitHub OIDC token, verified by GCP's WIF provider, scoped by attribute conditions to the repository ID and to the GitHub Environments that deploy to that project (dev: dev; stage: stage; prod: prod and prod-apply). GitHub adds the environment claim only to a job that passes the environment's deployment policy, so the environment rules decide which refs can reach each project: stage accepts main and prod-v*.*.* tags, prod and prod-apply accept only prod-v*.*.* tags, which only repository admins can create. A workflow on any other branch, or a job without a matching environment:, cannot authenticate to stage or prod, even with id-token: write. This holds where GitHub enforces deployment policies and rulesets: a private repository on GitHub Free has neither, so there any writer can reach stage and prod credentials (Protection Strategies). dev has no deployment policy, since pull request jobs plan against it.

What the WIF conditions block. Every job that can request an OIDC token (id-token: write) is a potential path to cloud credentials, whether it is a workflow a writer pushes on a branch or a compromised third-party action running inside an existing job. A job's steps can request a token for any provider's audience, so the provider's condition, not the workflow, decides what the token can reach:

Job dev stage prod Workflow on a branch, no environment: Rejected by WIF Rejected by WIF Rejected by WIF Step inside a pull request job (environment: dev) Credentials Rejected by WIF Rejected by WIF Workflow on a branch, environment: stage or prod n/a Blocked by GitHub Blocked by GitHub Merge to main, stage jobs n/a Credentials n/a Admin-pushed prod-v* tag, prod jobs n/a Credentials (used for registry lookups) Credentials

"Blocked by GitHub" means the environment's deployment policy refuses the ref, so the job never starts and never gets a token. Dev stays reachable from any branch by design; keep dev free of data and access that would matter if a pull request job were compromised.

One role set per project. Every environment admitted to a project's provider gets the same role set. Two consequences follow:

  • Promotion-tag runs authenticate to stage to resolve the image digest and read the stage registry, so they hold the full stage role set while needing only registry reads. Only admins can push the tag, and admins can already deploy stage by merging to main.
  • prod jobs (promote, plan, smoke) hold the same prod role set as prod-apply, before and after the approval. The approval trusts the plan artifact and summary from prod-plan, so a compromised dependency in that job could pass a malicious plan through the gate. Splitting roles between prod and prod-apply would not close this path, because the plan job still writes the artifact the apply runs. Review third-party actions and dependency changes as carefully as code that runs on prod credentials.

IAM database authentication, no passwords. The application service account authenticates to Cloud SQL using IAM identity (CLOUD_IAM_SERVICE_ACCOUNT user type, --auto-iam-authn proxy flag). No database password is stored, transmitted, or rotatable. The built-in postgres superuser has a random 30-character password with a strict validation policy — it exists only as a locked fallback, not for routine access.

Cross-project promotion uses WIF principals, not service accounts. Stage reads from dev's Artifact Registry, prod reads from stage's — but the IAM binding uses the WIF pool principal, not a service account. This avoids org policies that restrict cross-project service account usage and keeps the trust boundary at the identity pool level.

Dedicated smoke invoker, scoped to one service. The post-deploy smoke lane calls the live Cloud Run revision, which deploys --no-allow-unauthenticated and requires a Google-signed OIDC ID token whose audience is the service URL. The template provisions a separate invoker service account whose only grant is roles/run.invoker on the app Cloud Run service resource, not project-wide, so it can call that one service and nothing else. A caller's federated or user credentials cannot mint a service-audience ID token directly, so the lane impersonates the invoker SA in-process to generate one; the GitHub Actions WIF principal is granted roles/iam.serviceAccountOpenIdTokenCreator on the invoker SA so CI can mint the token, and local runs use the developer's own impersonation rights. The OpenID variant token-creator role is limited to the single iam.serviceAccounts.getOpenIdToken permission. Smoke access lives on its own identity, scoped to invocation and auditable independently of the runtime SA.

  • Source: terraform/bootstrap/module/gcp/main.tf (WIF pool, provider, attribute conditions)
  • Source: terraform/main/database.tf (IAM database user, password policy)
  • Source: terraform/main/smoke.tf (smoke invoker SA, resource-scoped run.invoker, WIF token-creator grant)
  • GCP docs: Workload Identity Federation, IAM database authentication, Cloud Run authentication
  • Guide: Infrastructure, Reference: Bootstrap

docs.title: Database Layer
docs.text:
Enforced Auth Proxy and TLS. connector_enforcement = "REQUIRED" rejects any connection not made through the Cloud SQL Auth Proxy. ssl_mode = "TRUSTED_CLIENT_CERTIFICATE_REQUIRED" enforces mutual TLS on every connection. These are server-side enforcements — a misconfigured client cannot bypass them.

Why both proxy enforcement and TLS? They protect different things. Connector enforcement ensures every connection is authenticated and authorized through GCP's control plane. TLS enforcement ensures the data channel is encrypted even within the VPC. Together, they prevent both unauthorized access and network-level eavesdropping.

Deletion protection and operational safety. Deletion protection is enabled for stage and prod environments, preventing accidental destruction of the database via Terraform or the console. Dev is left unprotected for easy teardown. Automated daily backups with point-in-time recovery provide a recovery path for data corruption or accidental deletes. The maintenance window is offset from the backup window to avoid contention — see Cloud SQL Scaling and Reliability for scheduling details. SQL Studio (data_api_access) is enabled in dev for debugging and disabled in stage/prod.

OAuth data protected in session state. For Agent applications requiring persistent user authentication, Session state is safe for storing sensitive values like OAuth access and refresh tokens because it inherits all database-layer protections:

  • Encryption at rest — Cloud SQL encrypts all data at rest with AES-256 using Google-managed keys by default (see also GCP default encryption). No configuration needed.
  • User isolation — ADK scopes sessions by user_id. One user's state keys are never visible to another user's session.
  • Automatic rotation — When using ADK's built-in OAuth2CredentialRefresher, OAuth tokens rotate automatically with no manual intervention required.
  • Value-safe logging — all credential-related logging uses key names and operation labels, never token values. Token contents do not appear in application logs, OTel traces, or debug output.

Important

When adding new logging, audit all logger.* calls in src/ to ensure token values are never logged. Follow the LoggingCallbacks._log_state_debug pattern (checks truthiness, logs keys only) for all state-related logging. Ensure logged tool_responses always contain only API data, not credentials: manage tokens in state, not tool responses.

  • Source: terraform/main/database.tf (connector enforcement, SSL mode, IAM auth flag, deletion protection, backups, maintenance)
  • Agent logging: LoggingCallbacks class in the package root callbacks.py module
  • GCP docs: Enforce Cloud SQL Auth Proxy, Configure SSL/TLS, Default encryption at rest
  • Reference: Cloud SQL Scaling and Reliability

docs.title: Compute Layer
docs.text:
Container-Optimized OS (COS) for the bastion. COS was chosen over a general-purpose Linux image (Ubuntu, Debian) for several properties that reduce the bastion's attack surface:

  • Verified boot with read-only root filesystem — the root filesystem is always mounted read-only, and its checksum is verified by the kernel on each boot. Malware cannot persist by modifying system binaries.
  • No package manager — containers package their own dependencies, so COS trims unnecessary packages to minimize the attack surface. An attacker with shell access cannot install additional software.
  • Minimal userland — COS includes only what is needed to run Docker containers. No compilers, interpreters, or network utilities that aid lateral movement.
  • Automatic security updates — the OS image is updated in its entirety (including the kernel) on an active-passive partition, not package-by-package. Updates take effect on reboot. COS requires explicit opt-in for automatic updates — the template sets cos-update-strategy = "update_enabled" in instance metadata to enable them.
  • Default-deny firewall — COS drops all incoming TCP/UDP connections except SSH on port 22. The cloud-init configuration explicitly opens only port 5432 for Auth Proxy traffic.
  • Docker-native — the Auth Proxy runs as a Docker container managed by systemd, not as a binary installed on the host. This provides process isolation and consistent versioning. The proxy image uses a floating major-version tag (cloud-sql-proxy:2) intentionally — this is a deliberate exception to the pinning principle, allowing automatic security patch pickup on container restart.

The bastion's sole purpose is running the Auth Proxy for developer access to Cloud SQL. COS enforces that constraint at the OS level — there is almost nothing else the instance can do.

Cloud Run Gen2 execution environment. Gen2 uses a full Linux VM with hardware-level isolation (KVM), providing stronger syscall compatibility than Gen1's gVisor-based sandbox.

  • Source: terraform/main/bastion.tf (COS image, no public IP, metadata)
  • Source: terraform/main/templates/bastion-cloud-init.yaml (iptables, systemd proxy service)
  • GCP docs: COS features and benefits, COS security overview (verified boot, read-only rootfs, default-deny firewall), COS automatic updates (active-passive partition scheme), COS host firewall, Cloud Run execution environments
  • Guide: Infrastructure

docs.title: Container Layer
docs.text:
Non-root execution. The Dockerfile creates a user (app:app, fixed UID and GID 10001) with no login shell (/usr/sbin/nologin) and switches to it before CMD. Running as non-root shrinks what a compromised process can do inside the container.

Multi-stage build. The uv binary and the dependency manifests stay in the builder stage; the runtime image contains only the Python base image, installed dependencies, and application source. Vulnerability scanners report on the final image's OS packages and Python dependencies, so keeping build tooling out of it keeps it off the report.

Pinned toolchain. The Dockerfile copies uv from an exact-version image tag, and dependencies install with --locked to enforce exact versions from uv.lock. The Python base image (python:X.Y-slim) is a floating tag: Docker Hub republishes it with OS and Python patch updates, so a rebuild can pick up a new base without a commit.

Immutable deployment by digest. CI/CD deploys Cloud Run revisions by image digest, not tag. A tag can be repointed; a digest cannot. This guarantees the exact image that was built and tested is what runs in production.

  • Source: Dockerfile (multi-stage build, non-root user, pinned uv)
  • Reference: Dockerfile Strategy

docs.title: Storage Layer
docs.text:
GCS public access prevention. The artifact service bucket enforces public_access_prevention = "enforced" and uniform_bucket_level_access = true, preventing accidental public exposure through object-level ACLs. Versioning is enabled for recovery from accidental overwrites.

  • Source: terraform/main/main.tf (GCS bucket configuration)
  • GCP docs: Public access prevention, Uniform bucket-level access

docs.title: Application Layer
docs.text:
Origin validation. ADK's origin check middleware blocks cross-origin state-changing requests (POST, PUT, DELETE) by validating the Origin header via exact string matching. This works alongside Starlette's CORS middleware. ALLOW_ORIGINS is validated at startup via a Pydantic field validator that rejects malformed JSON, non-array types, and empty values.

Fail-fast configuration. All environment variables are validated at startup through Pydantic's model_validate(). Missing or malformed configuration causes an immediate sys.exit(1) — the application never starts in a partially configured state.

Static analysis with security rules. Ruff's S rule set (flake8-bandit) runs in CI and locally, catching common security mistakes: hardcoded credentials, insecure function usage, and binding patterns. Suppressions require specific codes and justification (# noqa: S105 — test mock).

  • Source: src/<package>/config.py (Pydantic validation, ALLOW_ORIGINS)
  • GCP docs: Ruff flake8-bandit rules
  • Reference: ADK Origin Check Middleware, Code Quality

docs.title: Customer-Managed Encryption Keys (CMEK)
docs.text:
The template uses Google-managed encryption for all data at rest — Cloud SQL, GCS buckets, and Terraform state buckets. This is the GCP default and provides AES-256 encryption with Google-managed key rotation.

For organizations that require control over encryption key lifecycle (creation, rotation, revocation, access logging), GCP offers Customer-Managed Encryption Keys via Cloud KMS. CMEK gives you:

  • Key access auditing — Cloud Audit Logs record every use of the key, providing a trail for compliance
  • Key revocation — disabling or destroying the key renders encrypted data permanently inaccessible, useful for data disposal requirements
  • Key rotation control — set your own rotation schedule rather than relying on Google's
  • Separation of duties — key management and data access are controlled by different IAM roles

Where to apply CMEK in this project:

Resource Terraform Field Documentation Cloud SQL instance settings.disk_encryption_key_name Cloud SQL CMEK GCS buckets (artifact service) encryption.default_kms_key_name GCS CMEK Terraform state buckets encryption.default_kms_key_name Same as GCS Bastion boot disk (COS) boot_disk.kms_key_self_link Compute Engine CMEK Artifact Registry (bootstrap) kms_key_name Artifact Registry CMEK Vertex AI Agent Engine encryption_spec Vertex AI CMEK

Getting started: Create a Cloud KMS keyring and crypto key in the same region as your resources, grant the relevant service agents the roles/cloudkms.cryptoKeyEncrypterDecrypter role, then reference the key in the Terraform fields above. Each GCP service uses a different service agent — consult the linked documentation for the specific principal.

Important

CMEK adds operational complexity: key deletion is irreversible (data loss), key rotation requires planning, and cross-region keys have latency implications. Evaluate whether your compliance requirements mandate CMEK before adopting it.

docs.title: Smoke Tests
docs.text: The smoke lane: post-deploy checks against a live Cloud Run revision.

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
The smoke lane (tests/smoke/) hits the live deployed Cloud Run service URL after terraform apply to confirm a freshly deployed revision actually serves end to end. Unlike the integration lane, which builds the app in-process via httpx ASGITransport, nothing here is substituted: the request crosses the real network, the Auth Proxy sidecar, and Cloud SQL. The L2 turn invokes the real model, but the lane is still a deterministic gate. Behavioral correctness stays owned by the eval lane, pre-deploy wiring by the integration lane.

The lane runs only by explicit path (uv run pytest tests/smoke).

docs.title: What each layer catches
docs.text:
Before any check runs, the client fixture polls /health until the revision serves, so cold-start latency on a freshly deployed revision is absorbed once and the checks run with their normal timeout. The lane is a single test module with no conftest.

Checks run cheapest-first, each a distinct failure class so a failure localizes the broken subsystem:

  • L0 liveness: GET /health -> 200. The revision serves HTTP at all.
  • L1 session create: create a session, read it back -> 200. Cloud SQL is reachable through the Auth Proxy sidecar over VPC egress, and a session row persists. Deterministic, no model. A module-scoped fixture owns the create so teardown deletes the row unconditionally even when a later check fails.
  • L2 thin agent turn: POST /run_sse with a trivial prompt, parse the SSE event stream, and assert at least one event carries a text part. The real model is invoked, but the assertion checks only that a text part returned, never what it says, so the check is robust to the model's stochastic output and carries no LLM-judge dependency.
  • L3 cleanup: delete the smoke session, then a follow-up GET returns 404. Proves the delete path and leaves no residue.

docs.title: How authentication works
docs.text:
The service deploys --no-allow-unauthenticated, so Cloud Run requires a Google-signed OIDC ID token whose audience is the service URL. A caller's own credentials (a developer's gcloud login, or the CI WIF principal) cannot mint that token directly, so the lane impersonates a dedicated invoker service account to generate it. Impersonation runs in-process with impersonated_credentials.IDTokenCredentials, sourced from the caller's own Application Default Credentials, so the same test code works locally and in CI and no token is passed through the environment:

  • Locally: set your ADC using gcloud. Run gcloud auth application-default login once if you have not. Your principal needs permission to mint ID tokens as the invoker SA; grant yourself roles/iam.serviceAccountOpenIdTokenCreator (it includes only the iam.serviceAccounts.getOpenIdToken permission) on the invoker SA.
  • In CI: the GitHub Actions WIF principal, which terraform/main/smoke.tf grants roles/iam.serviceAccountOpenIdTokenCreator on the invoker SA.

The invoker SA is a least-privilege identity distinct from the runtime app SA, holding only roles/run.invoker on the app's Cloud Run service. The test client reads the invoker SA email from SMOKE_INVOKER_SA, mints the ID token by impersonation, and sends it as Authorization: Bearer. See Security Posture for the identity model.

docs.title: Run it locally
docs.text:
The smoke lane targets a live deployed URL and reads two env vars: SMOKE_BASE_URL (the deployed service URL) and SMOKE_INVOKER_SA (the invoker SA email the client impersonates). Both are Terraform outputs (smoke_target_url, smoke_invoker_service_account_email), available from the GitHub Actions apply job summary (gh run view <run-id>) or the Cloud Console (the Cloud Run service URL; the SA under IAM & Admin). If you have the main module initialized locally, read them with terraform output:

SMOKE_BASE_URL="$(terraform -chdir=terraform/main output -raw smoke_target_url)" \
SMOKE_INVOKER_SA="$(terraform -chdir=terraform/main output -raw smoke_invoker_service_account_email)" \
  uv run pytest tests/smoke

Both are test-harness variables, not application runtime config, so they live here rather than in docs/environment-variables.md. No token env var is needed: the client mints the ID token in-process from your gcloud ADC.

docs.title: How CI runs it post-deploy
docs.text:
The smoke.yml reusable workflow authenticates to GCP via WIF and runs uv run pytest tests/smoke with SMOKE_BASE_URL and SMOKE_INVOKER_SA set, surfacing pass/fail in the GitHub job summary. The test impersonates the SA in-process, so no token crosses the environment. The service URL and invoker SA email come from terraform-plan-apply.yml outputs (smoke_target_url, smoke_invoker_service_account_email), threaded through ci-cd.yml. The smoke test workflow is called after each environment apply — dev-smoke after dev-apply on merge, and in production mode stage-smoke after stage-apply on merge and prod-smoke after prod-apply on tag. This runs post-deploy against the live revision, not in the PR gate.

docs.title: Testing Strategy
docs.text: The lane taxonomy and the unit-test guide; the specialized lanes link to their own references.

docs.title: Test Lanes
docs.text:
A test's lane is decided by its runtime requirements and determinism, not by how many components it touches.

Lane Needs Deterministic Cost Local command unit in-process only (mocks at boundaries) yes free/fast uv run pytest (default) integration real external resource (Postgres) yes slower, no LLM/cloud uv run pytest tests/integration smoke a live deployed URL yes needs a deploy uv run pytest tests/smoke eval the real LLM deterministic gate yes; judge gate no costs money uv run pytest tests/eval

The unit, integration, and smoke lanes never call the live model; the eval lane does. Evals are still a test shape, so the lane lives under tests/ alongside the others — pytest uses importlib import mode (location-agnostic), and adk eval takes explicit evalset and config filepaths, so nothing depends on where the lane sits. Non-unit lanes run by explicit path, both locally and in CI — the command or CI job is the selector. testpaths = ["tests/unit"] in pyproject.toml scopes a bare uv run pytest to the fast, free, deterministic lane so it can't accidentally require Postgres. An explicit path argument overrides it.

Only the unit lane runs --cov with the 100% gate.

Live output: pytest captures output and shows it only for failing tests. Two flags stream it as the run happens, and they cover different streams:

  • -s turns off capture, so anything printed to stdout appears live. In the eval lane that is ADK's own output: the logging plugin's per-event lines, progress bars, and results tables. Both CI eval steps pass it.
  • --log-cli-level=INFO (lifecycle) or --log-cli-level=DEBUG (full detail) streams Python log records from the logging module, like the template's callbacks and library internals, in the timestamped format pyproject.toml sets. The flag is the switch; nothing streams by default. DEBUG includes model request and response content, so keep it out of CI logs for a fork with real user data.

Eval-lane detail: Agent Evals "Watching eval logs live".

uv run pytest tests/integration --log-cli-level=INFO

docs.title: Specialized Lanes
docs.text:
The rest of this guide covers the unit lane. The non-unit lanes each carry their own reference doc:

  • Integration (tests/integration/) — the real FastAPI app against a real Postgres session service, no mocks. See Integration Tests.
  • Smoke (tests/smoke/) — assertions against a live deployed URL, run post-deploy against a freshly applied Cloud Run revision. See Smoke Tests.
  • Eval (tests/eval/) — real agent behavior scored against committed eval sets; the only lane that catches LLM behavioral regression. Cases split by pytest marker, and each marker is a CI gate: deterministic (exact tool-trajectory + ROUGE match) gates every PR, and judge (LLM-judged, non-deterministic) gates every merge to main, blocking in production mode. Inference runs the full App and its plugins, so evals score the same agent the deployed server runs. tests/unit/test_eval_artifacts.py schema-checks the eval data in the unit lane, with no LLM cost. See Agent Evals.

docs.title: Coverage Requirements
docs.text:
100% coverage required on production code.

Included: - All code in src/ except explicitly excluded files (see below)

Excluded: - server.py (FastAPI entrypoint - validate server behavior with integration tests) - **/agent.py (pure ADK configuration - tests are the upstream project's responsibility) - **/prompt.py (prompt templates - validate agent behavior with evaluations) - **/__init__.py (module initialization)

docs.title: Directory Structure
docs.text:
Lanes are top-level directories; unit test modules mirror source structure:

tests/
  eval/                          # LLM eval lane (real model, deterministic + judge markers)
  unit/
    conftest.py                  # Shared fixtures, mocks, and unit test environment setup
    test_callbacks.py            # Tests for src/your_agent/callbacks.py
    test_tools.py                # Tests for src/your_agent/tools.py
    test_config.py               # Tests for src/your_agent/config.py
    ...
  integration/                   # Postgres + FastAPI lane
    conftest.py                  # Docker setup for testcontainers only
    test_server_integration.py   # Fixtures, mocks, and tests
  smoke/                         # Live deployed-URL lane

Each lane owns its credential posture: the unit lane's tests/unit/conftest.py mocks credentials within the pytest_configure hook; the integration lane mocks credentials in an autouse session fixture; the smoke lane uses real credentials. The eval lane loads the real .env itself (an autouse fixture in the test module). There is deliberately no shared tests/conftest.py — its absence keeps the unit lane's credential mocking out of the eval and smoke lanes, which run against real credentials.

docs.title: Naming Conventions
docs.text:
• Files: test module path mirrors source path: src/<pkg>/config.py → tests/unit/test_config.py; nested source paths flatten with underscores (<pkg>/sub/foo.py → test_sub_foo.py)
  • Functions: test_<what>_<condition>_<expected>
  • Classes: Group related tests for the same module/class (style preference)

docs.title: Shared Fixtures
docs.text: All reusable unit-lane fixtures go in tests/unit/conftest.py: - Type hint fixture definitions with both parameters and return types - Use pytest-mock type aliases for returns: MockType, AsyncMockType - Factory pattern (not context managers)

docs.title: Package-Name Discovery
docs.text:
Lanes that reference the source package resolve its name at runtime from src/ instead of hard-coding it: next(SRC_DIR.glob("*/__init__.py")).parent.name. The unit conftest.py uses it for mock patch targets, the integration lane for APP_NAME, and the eval lane for AGENT_MODULE (resolving SRC_DIR as Path(__file__).parents[2]). A renamed fork reuses every lane with no edits, and init_template.py skips the unit conftest because it carries no literal package name.

The bare next() is intentional. The template has exactly one package under src/, so a violation raises StopIteration at import with a traceback on the exact line. A guard would trade one crash for another and would not catch the multiple-package case, where next() takes the first match. Discovery is duplicated per lane because there is no shared tests/conftest.py to hold it.

docs.title: Test Double Naming
docs.text:
Test double classes and fixtures follow a strict naming convention (established in tests/unit/conftest.py):

Kind Prefix Example Returns Test double class Mock MockState, MockOAuthContextStore — (defined in conftest) Instance fixture mock_ mock_state, mock_chat_client Single mock instance Factory fixture create_mock_ create_mock_state, create_mock_oauth_store Callable that builds instances Convenience fixture (none) oauth_flow_config, valid_server_env Real objects / test data

Factory fixtures use _factory as their inner function name:

@pytest.fixture
def create_mock_state() -> Callable[..., MockState]:
    def _factory(data: dict | None = None) -> MockState:
        return MockState(data)

    return _factory

docs.title: Type Hints
docs.text:
Fixture definitions (strict in conftest.py): 

from pytest_mock import MockerFixture
from pytest_mock.plugin import MockType


@pytest.fixture
def mock_session(mocker: MockerFixture) -> MockType:
    """Create a mock ADK session."""
    return mocker.MagicMock(spec=...)

Test functions (relaxed): - Don't type hint custom fixtures (pytest handles DI by name) - Optional type hints on built-in fixtures for IDE support

docs.title: Environment Mocking
docs.text:
No base env vars in pytest_configure(): No module in the test import graph reads env vars at module level. server.py does (module-level initialize_environment()), but it's never imported during collection (PEP 562 lazy loading, coverage-excluded). Environment variables are set in test fixtures using mocker.patch.dict:

def test_config_with_custom_region(mocker: MockerFixture) -> None:
    """Test configuration with non-default region."""
    mocker.patch.dict(os.environ, {"GOOGLE_CLOUD_LOCATION": "us-west1"})
    # Test config loading with custom region

ServerEnv tests build settings through the isolated_environ factory fixture, which sets os.environ to exactly the given variables and replaces the config module's load_dotenv with a no-op, so neither the developer's shell nor a local .env leaks in. Tests that exercise .env loading use the create_dotenv factory, which writes a temporary .env and points load_dotenv at it.

If a future import chain triggers env var reads at collection time, add direct os.environ assignments in pytest_configure() (see section below).

docs.title: Using Conftest Fixtures
docs.text: Prefer fixtures from conftest.py for standard mocks: - mock_state - ADK state object - mock_session - ADK session - mock_context - ReadonlyContext with user_id

docs.title: Never Import Mock Classes
docs.text: Never import mock classes directly in test files. Always use or add a fixture in conftest.py. For edge cases requiring custom internal structure, add a specific named fixture (e.g., mock_event_non_text_content) rather than importing the class.

docs.title: Mirror Real Interfaces
docs.text: ADK mocks must exactly mirror real ADK interfaces: - Use spec= parameter to enforce interface - Include all properties and methods used in code - Match return types and signatures

docs.title: pytest_configure()
docs.text:
Special case: unittest.mock before pytest-mock available

pytest_configure() runs before test collection, so pytest-mock isn't available yet. Use unittest.mock here for setup that must happen before tests load:

def pytest_configure() -> None:
    """Configure test environment before test collection."""
    from unittest.mock import Mock, patch

    # Patch google.auth.default to prevent ADC lookup
    mock_creds = Mock(token="fake", valid=True, expired=False)
    patch("google.auth.default", return_value=(mock_creds, "test-project")).start()
    patch(
        "google.auth._default.default", return_value=(mock_creds, "test-project")
    ).start()

    # Environment variables: No module in the test import graph reads env vars at
    # module level. server.py does (initialize_environment()), but it's
    # never imported during collection (PEP 562 lazy loading, coverage-excluded).
    # If a future import chain triggers env var reads at collection time, set
    # defaults here using direct assignment:
    # import os
    # os.environ["KEY"] = "value"

See tests/unit/conftest.py for the complete implementation with detailed lifecycle comments.

docs.title: Validation Timing
docs.text:
Pydantic validates at model creation, not at property access:

# Validation happens here ✓
config = ServerEnv.model_validate(env_dict)

# NOT here ✗
value = config.some_property

docs.title: Testing Validation
docs.text:
Expect ValidationError at model creation:

import pytest
from pydantic import ValidationError


def test_config_invalid_project_id():
    """Test that empty project ID raises validation error."""
    env_dict = {"GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT": ""}

    with pytest.raises(ValidationError):
        ServerEnv.model_validate(env_dict)

docs.title: Behaviors
docs.text: Test function outputs and state changes: - Return values are correct - State is modified as expected - Side effects occur (logging, callbacks)

docs.title: Error Conditions
docs.text: Test invalid inputs and edge cases: - Invalid parameter types - Missing required values - Boundary conditions (empty, max, negative)

docs.title: Integration Points
docs.text: App and agent wiring (callbacks registered, tools attached, configuration flow) is validated by the integration lane against a real server.

docs.title: Mypy Scope
docs.text: mypy checks tests/ alongside src/ in strict mode. A tests.* override relaxes only fixture-parameter annotations and duck-typed mock arguments, and a tests.*.conftest override re-enables the annotation checks so fixture definitions stay fully typed. The override and the test patterns it shapes are in Code Quality → Test Suite Typing Strategy.

docs.title: Running Tests
docs.text:
# Unit lane (default) with full coverage report
uv run pytest --cov --cov-report=term-missing

# HTML report for detailed view
uv run pytest --cov --cov-report=html
open htmlcov/index.html

# Other lanes by explicit path
uv run pytest tests/integration
uv run pytest tests/smoke
uv run pytest tests/eval

# Specific tests
uv run pytest tests/unit/test_callbacks.py -v
uv run pytest tests/unit/test_file.py::test_name -v

# Watch mode (requires pytest-watch)
uv run ptw
